The Scot eyed him for a moment, and then, looking him full in the face, remarked, " Mau, that's a peety, as ye hae sae gran' accommodation! -- The new barito,ne, Josef Claus, who has already Won`his Way Co Tifiblic favour on the concert plat- form; itra-tiotremian-irr the iiteral-senze;--audrcom es- from a very musical family. In boy liond he watt he fortunate possessor of a pure and beautiful mezzo- soprano, and sang with a fervour and intensity rare at that early age. He appeared at concerts in his native•conntry, and toured the United States and Havana as a youthful. prodigy. Serious study was commenced at nineteen, when he altered the Vienna Imperial Conservatoire as a pupil of the great teacher of singing, Rokitanski. Fired with desire to appear in opera, ,he subsequently went to Italy and studied for two, years with the famous Lamperti before making his d6but in "1 Promessi Sposi, his success in which secured him engage- ments at Home, Vienna, Genoa, and other cities. His repertoire includes over twenty operas, but his best parts are Valentine in "Faust," Antonio in Donizetti's "Linda," Alfonso in "La Favorita,"
I cut m;-

and Verdi's great roles for baritone. Like most artistes. he was anxious to visit England,and accor- dingly came over last season. It is to be hoped that his splendid voice may be beard in open before he leaves us.

Dr. Wordsworth's long tenure of the bishopric of St. Andrews has come to an end. The late bishop had held the office since 185.3,when he resigned the wardenship of Glenalmond College. He came of a •remarkable family. His father waE! the most dis- tinguished classical scholar of his year at Cam- bridge; his uncle was William Wordsworth the poet. and his brother was the Bishop ofiLincoln,and his nephew is the present Bishop of Salisbury.

Bishop Wordsworth was a famous athlete in his day. Re used to tell with pride that he played in the first Harrow and Winchester cricket match in 1825, when he took nine Winchester wickets. Car- dinal Manning was one of the Winchester team on t hat occasion. Two years later he played for Ox- ford in the first inter-University match, and in the following year he played again, and formed one of the Oxford crew in the first University boat raca. The bishop was a considerable author. He had published works on Shakespeare, as well as histo- ries of the Scottish Church and the Reformation. Perhaps his best known work is the excellent "Christian Boybood in a Public Schgol," thougli his name is likely to be handed down tb future ;One- rations chiefly as the compiler of a'areek grammar.

• Thera was a good assembly at the Democratic Club on Saturday evening to do honour toqdr. Fletcher, editor of the " Daily Chronicle." !Mr. Tom Mann was in thp chair and Mrs. Tom Minn, too, was there; Mr. Blair, the secretary, and Mrs. Blair; Mr. Stapley, the candidate who made so good a fight at Brixton, and Mrs, Stapley ; Mr. W. M. Thompson, with his.. fine dark eyes and keen countenance ; Herbert Burrows, watchful and thoughtful ; and many another man and woman well known in the fields of journalism, politics;and literature. Professor Stuart Was among the guests, as were Mr. ShiPton, who represented the old trade unionism, and spoke well up for it too and for the new, Miirrison Lavitison, Scotch to the backbone, and Mr. Massingham 'thoroughly enjoying the tri- umph of his chief.

Mr, Fletcher ia a man whom one cannot easily forget, if once one has seen him. A firmly-built, active man, with gray, hair, erey bit a journalist, keen, quiet, observant., one would not have thought itt fir,t sight that he had the gifts of a real Orator, too. But nevertheless he has, and the speech he Made will remain long impressed on the memory of those who heard it. There wae a breadth of sympathy,. a wide grasp of great pioblems, a firm- ness and boldness linked with a delicacy of touch. which 'charmed and captivated his audience, and led tfieria, as Professor Stuart expressed 'in his few words of kindly appreciation of the good work of Mr. Fletcher and - his staff; to recognise • whence came the inspiration of the great journalover which Mr. Fletcher presides.

Mr. Fletcher is, like so many eminent journalists, a native of East Anglia. He'studied wheti,)i young Man at St. Andrews .Vniver'Sity, in Scotland. • Ile has found his way back to East Anglia again, for lie has a house near Chelmsford, where be retires whenever he can. Like not a few other busy men, he is a lover of the country. A fine view is got from Ins home, and there his cattle, for he is a farmer by inclination, give him a pleasant relief from the hard work of Fleet-st.

Mr. Cecil Rhodes is no ladies' man, says a gossip, and has a habit of ignoring the fair sex whenever he can. He dellineci altogethrr at the meeting in Canon-st. Uote4 the other day, to acknowledge the presence of several ladies amcing the audience. In private life be pursues 'the same.tactics, only in a more marked degree. Thus he, ie:ry seldom goes into ladies' society, and will not suffer the presence if a aingle female domestic in his establishment. The' last peculiarity may, however,find explanation in the fact that his men servants are by far the most capable in Cape Town. His boy Tony, in particular, who is a Kaffir half caste, possesses a I.),•rfect genius for household work, and is in addi- tion devotedly attached loins master.

Lord Roseberry, following the precedent of Mr. Asquith, is at present in Dublin on a visit at the Chid Secretary's Lodge• With Mr.. John Morley. The Dublin papers say that Mr. Morley took Lord Rosebery tu see the old Irish Houses of Parliament. Thi4 is scarcely, accurate. The 'lrish House of Lords is in its appearance of structure exactly the titaness it was at the time of the Union. except that, the throne frbm which the' LordZieutenant used to deliver speeehes is removed; and in its plies a statue of George 111, has been erected. The Cham- ber in which the Mai House of Commons sat; has, Nowever, ceased to exist. When the Irish Parlia- ment House was given t. the directors of ths Bank of Ireland, Mr. Abbott, who wits then Chief Secre- tary for Ireland, and afterwards Speaker of the Rouse of Commons, insisted on its demolition with the view of 'effacing as far as possible the recol- lection of the popular assembly' 'front the people's minds.

Jay Gould extorted unquestioning compliance with his orders from all under his influence or con- trol. A young Englishman landed in New York with a: letter of introduction to Gould from a cable magnate in London. The arch millionaire gave him a note to the manager of the Elevated Railway in New York, asking the latter to give him a station- mastership. There was no such position vacant 'at the moment, and the immigrant brought back a message to Gould to that effect. The Wall-st. king requested his proteg6 to call at the manager's office early next morning, The ',Englishman did as directed, and immediately received charge of one of the mostimportatit stations on the railway. Gould had made a vacancy in the interval.:

31.1tibot, the new leader of the French Cabibet,is in his fiftieth year. He is a tall man of aristocra- tic appearance, and is a personal friend or Lord Dufferin, at whose receptions he is invariably to be met. As Minister of Foreign Affairs in the two preceding Cabinets he showed great moderatiou and elevation of character. ' His •accession to the chief power is therefore popular, especially at this critical period when the Panama embroilment makes the task of governing no easy problem. Two ot the new members of the Ribot Cabinet—MM. Dupuy and Siegfried, both middle-aged men—have recommendations in their favour. The former has been an enlightened professor of the university, and the latter a wealthy philanthropist.

Mr. Raymond Blathwayt, the interviewer, says the" Novel Review," was at one time a clergyman, starting his clerical career in Trinidad. After his return to England he felt that the church was not his vocation, and resigned the curacy he held at Barking. In the period of idleness which followed this step, the opportunity of interviewing Mr. William Black, the novejist, presented itself. Mr. Blathwayt seized it eagerly, and the " Pall Mall Gazette' published the result. Since that time— three years ago— novelists of every degree have been laid under contribution for the breezy and well informed interviews he writes from time to ' time. Mark Twain, Hardy, Howell, Frank Stock- ton, Robert Barr, Hall Caine. Grant Allen, Fronde, Walter Besant, and James Russell Lowell are amongst the many men of whom Mr. Blathwayt has made" copy."

The official announcement that the Queen has appointed Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., to be fourth Charity Commissioner for England and Wales marks another stage in an unusually promising career. The young Oxford man, who represents his native Merioneth- shire in the House of Commons, and had already been appointed a Junior Lord of the Treasury in Mr. Gladstone's Government, is known to many as the" uncrowned King of Wales," and to many more as a politician of unusual earnestness and power.

His unrivalled grasp of the two most urgent politi- cal problems of Wales—the land question and dis- establishiment--has not prevented_ him horn bring- ing such keeness as onlya true patriotism can inspire to the solution of the third problem which at presen6 -eTiffigelitliTa`most -spirited-efforts-of-Your g W ales, namely 'education,

It is, if we mistake not, mainly in the, last-aarned department that Mr. Ellies new office will add strength to his arm and make him a still more use- ful ally of men like Mr. Ellis Edwards, of Bain, and Mr. 0. M. Edwards, of Oxford, to whose enthusiasm for the highest ideals future generations of ' their countrymen will be so deeply indebted.

ST. HELENS AND THE LOCAL GOV- ERNMENT BOARD, • - GREAT SEWAGE SCHEME. EXTENSION OF THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL. On Thurrday, a deputation from the St. Helens Corporation, consisting of the Mayor (Mr. A, Sin- clair, J.P.,) Alderman J. C. Gamble (chairman of the Finance Committee), Alderman It. Pilkington (chairman of the Parliamentary Committee), Coun- cillor J. Forster, (chairman af the Health Conunittee), CouncillorJ. Massey, Mr. W. J. Jeeves (Town Clerk), Mr. George J. C. Broom, M.1.C.E.. (borough surveyor), and Dr. Robertson (assistant medical officer of health), waited upon the Local Government Board and explained the views of the Corporation regarding several schemes vitally affecting the borough. First of these is the completion of the main sewer and the vexed question of the state of the brook a'ter emerg- ing from the borough at the Double Locks in 'Parr. Nome years since the Corporation applied to the Local Government Board for power to borrow money to con- struct a sewer, but the central authority then desired to see a complete system of sewage carried out. There had been frequent epidemics of typhoid fever, the principal locality of the disease being along the line of the brook into which the sewage flowed. A complete system such las would have met the wishes of Mr. Ritchie's Local 1 Government Board would have involved an expenditure of from £30,000 to £40,000, and the Council.w were not prepared to launch out to such an extent. The matter lLy in abeyance, and, meanwhile, it was decided to proceed slowly in the direction indicated. The borough surveyor prepared plans for an intercepting sewer to be constructed through streets running as nearly as possible parallel with the brook, but at a greater depth ; aad as the gas estate yielded an annual profit, it was decided to appropriate it to this purpose. A contract was signed for £17,373, aid the sewer was constructed from Spray's Bridge, on the Eccleston and Knowsley side of the town, to Ashc- 4ft's Bridge, in Parr, where it again turned into the opf brook. The work cost, with extras,about £lB,OOO, t the effect has been an improvement in the health of the tdwn. This summer the cases of typhoid fever have been few and the disease had not assumed the nature of an epidemic. The death- , Atte has been lower, as shown in the monthly compara- tive statements -of the medical officers. But while this ' satisfactory state of things has been going on the resi- dents of Parr have strongly objected to the sewage run- ning through the district to the open. The scheme em- braced two sections, one of which had been completed, and the other was, to carry the sewage forward from Ashcroft'a Bridge -to the Double Lock, a distance of a mile. Then lying "in abeyance—hinted at, but shelved , on account of the cost—Was the idea of putting down filtering tanks, and treating the sewage before it flowed further along the Sankey Brook, through the country to the Mersey. At a Govern- ment inquiry held in January last into an application made to extend the borough, the sewage system was fully dealt with. Dr. Robertson said he had made most careful experiments within the previous six months,and found thtit the perfect system of disinfection was going ini by the chemical drainage mixing with the sewage ; in fact, it was more perfect than any outfall works could produce. The chemicals killed tia bacteria and made the refuse innocuous to life. The decision of .the Local Government Board was conveyed in the follow- ing form t—" The Board have determined to defer the further consideration of the question until proper provision has been made for the purification of ' the sewage of the borough before its discharge into Sankey Brook." The Corporation is now promoting a bill in Parliament seeking for powers to extend the borough boundaries so as to enclose portions of the I townships of Eccleston and Windle, the area being similar to that included in the recent application to the Lcol Government Board, and for many other purposes. Such an application could not be successful until the question of the sewage was disposed of; hence the object of the deputation on Thursday. It seems now to be a question whether the present Local Government Board will approve of the extension of the sewer to the boundary di the borough with- out any further additional w.rlts, or whether they will require filtering beds to be constructed, the principal cost of which would be very large, and in con- nection with which a large sum for maintenance would be absorbed annually. The deputation had also another matter in hand, and that was to confer with the o.Mcials of the Local Government Board on the extension of the Isolation Hospital at reasley Cross. The present hospi- tal consists of . a private' house, which was pur- chased so:pe years ago for the purpose, and with the stable, coachhouse, &c., which were at consider- able cost prepared as wards, will accommodate six- teen patients. In face of any epidemic that may break • chit, such as smallpox, typhoid, or scarlet fever, the sani- tary authority are not in a position to receive more patients than are suffering from one particular disease, and even then the accommodation is too limited for a population of over 70,000. During the prevailing epide- mic of smallpox in Warrington and other places in West Lancashire, and the fact that the disease made its ap- pearance in St. Helens,a temporary wooden building was erected pending an inquiry by the Local Government Board into an application to spend £2,500 to perma- nently provide for an additional 26 beds. .

His grease box was lying clod& beside him. The driver Whistled several ,times-before coming up to -the -waggons, There were 'no rules on the Ship Canal with reference to engines approaching waggons. Cross-examined by Mr. Davies, witness said the fetters were not obliged to go under- neath a waggon in the course of their duties. A lad 14 years of age,natned Isherwood said he was employed along with the deceased in greasing the waggons in ques- tion on Sattirday.The deceased Was grehelag the end wag- gon.—ln reply to the coroner, he said that fatters were obliged to go underneath a waggon when the axle be- came hot. Witness was knocked doWn but was not hurt. They received no warning that the engine was coming. —ln reply to tho Coroner, this witness also stated that the axle coed net be 'gratified 'unless the fatter went underneath the,waggons.--Thomas Bennott,a" slasher" on the Sbip;C;ankl, said ha hp charge of the boys who were employed at fatting on the Stockton Heath section. He gave them all special instructions, and read out+ a rule to the deceaso,l to the effect that he was forbidden toga underneath a waggon while fatting: The jury re- turned a verdict of " Accidental death," and expressed the opinion that the driver Of the engine " Timperley " and the Ship Canal!Company had been-guilty of gross negligence.—The Coroner remarked that the driver had certainly been guilty of negligence in approaching so near to the waggons in front of hire. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred there was always someone employed in greasing, &c.,at waggons which were at a standstill. It was his opinion that drivers of engines ought to receive certain instructions on this matter. Further, he did not think that a lad would be able to grease the axle of a waggon properly unless he went underneath.—Mr. Percy Davies said the Ship Canal Company were not aware of the laxity, if laxity there/ was,oa.the part of drivers and others on the Ship Canal works. They would see that these matters were attended to. in future.

div.head: MEXICAN IRON MOUNTAIN.
div.p: A MEXICAN IRON MOUNTAIN.

celebrated iron mountain at Durange, Mexico, known as the Cerro del Meicado, has (says " Iron") been sold by the Durange Steel and Iron Company of Des Moines, lowa, to Mr. C. P. Hunt- ingdon, of the Southern Pacific and Mexican Inter- national Railways, who, it is 'believed, intends to establish large iron and steel works in proximity to Du:al:we City. The Cerro del Mercado is a mass of iron ore, one mile long, one-third of a mile wide, and rising from 400 ft, to 650 ft. above the level of the plain on which it is situated. Its existence has been known for a considerable period. In was dis- covered by the Spaniards early in the 16th century, and in 1558 an expedition was despatched to ex- amine it, owing more, as is usually the case, to the reports that it contained gold and. silver than from. any belief that an iron property, •however rich, could then be profitably exploited. No discoveries of the precious metals being made, it was, like the gigantic Australian. ferriferous deposit, Iron Monarch, abandoned for the time being ; and it was not until after the independance ot Mexico had been declared that an English company acquired the mine and the right to establish ironworks near it, when actual development work, and the pro- duction cf pig iron was comrr enced on a'compara- tively large scale. Weidner, who investigated the property for the Mexican government exactly 300 years after the Castilian experts had examined it, estimated the hill to contain 250.000,000 tons of 50 per cent ore.

div.head: HUMOURS OF IRISH MATCH /CAKING.
div.p: HUMOURS OF IRISH MATCH /CAKING.

Irishmen make good husbands as a rule; hut there is singularly little romance in their usual I methods of choosing a partner. One would hardly expect, says the Standard," such a state of things as this, when one remembers the wealth of their love poetry; but it is a fact, nevertheless, that the ' sort of peotry the average young Pat prefers in real life is that which brings in its train houseeand land, or in default of these, cows and pigs, and those other two or four footed accessories which add to the competeness and happiness of a country . cottage. An Englishman in love holds these things in very poor account. He would be a curious spe- cimen of the race who should pass over a pretty girl in the heydey of her, charms and place his invaluable affections upon an antiquated Venus twice her age because she can bring him a comfort- able acre of land for the potatoes. Irishmen will do this, and indeed, make a practice of it. We have known of a marriage brok •n off at the church door because of a very little filthy lucre. A wed- ding had been arrangtki between a young couple by their respective parents ; the day was fixed and friends invited ; and the whole party in half-a-dozen cars, reached the chapel. Just as they stopped 'outside to arrange the order of going in, the father of another girl came to tie bridegroom and offered him his daughter, with £lO more fortune than the youth was getting with the one be was " promised to." " Done" said the. ' unfeeling wretch, and straightway discarded his first love and married the other girl instead. We never heard that he was horsewhipped ; indeed, the guests seem t have regarded the affair as nothing out of,the ordinary. , his consoling, however, to know that the jilted girls ' bonnet was not made in vain. " There's a girl of the ' Scanlon's getting Married to-day." said a shopwoman' to ' her customer," but I made her bonnet a couple of years I ago." " Indeed that's strange," replied the customer. ". How did it all happen ?" " Well " .was the, reply, " they were on their way to the chapel, when there was some little difference, and the match was broken off, but, like a sensible girl, she kept the bonnet, and now, you,See, it comes in handy." Not long ago a certain ; well-to-do farmer, in one of the provinces of Ulster, had I been dividing his attentions pretty equally between two fairWonien—one a widow and the otheisthe Only (laugh- ter of a rich pig jobber. The cause of this vacillisti ! wan that the qualification of both the candidates were , identical. Will it be believed that the man did net agreo to take the young and pretty girl until her father had put another pig in her scale ? As already hinted, mar- , riages are very frequently arranged between the parents of both the parties interested, and it often .happens in ' the South ot Ireland that a groom does not see his bride ' ' until brought face to face with her at church. In one ' such case as this the lady had the misfortune to have lost one eye. " Faix,'! said the young man after sur- veying her for the first time, " I'll marry no girl unless her eyes are there." And lie did not marry her. Match- making is a regular institution in the South of Ireland, and, it would seem, in some parts of tne North. There are professional matchmakers in every -district, who make it their business to find out the fortuneS'of, arid get suitable partners for, all the eligible young people of both sexes for miles round. There is an approved season of the year for the carrying on of negotiations. It is known as ShroVetide, and extends from Christmas to Shrove Tuesday, the three weeks immediately preceding Lent being the busy time. When the well-to-do parents of a marriageable son find themselves getting on in years,and unable to look after the farm and all connected with it, they tell their boy that he must take a wife,and straight- way send for their friend the znatialunaker. The old peo- ple in such eases, we are assured, are quite content to , give up the farm to their eon, seldom asking anything beyond their support and a seat in the chimney corner of the old home for the rest of their days. Herein they are more fortunate than Bing Lear under parallel cir- cumstances. The son who obtains the house and farm as practically his own is considered well off, therefore, the girl be marries must have money equal, or nearly equal to his—if not in hard cash, then in cattle, which are a very old form of currency. When everything has been arranged between the parents on both aides,the das for the marriage is fixed, and the marriage money made up for ths priest. It will be easily understood, as already pointed out, that by this order of procedure, the partly- mcst concerned may not be thrown into one another's' way until, perhaps, the day that is to make them one, Near Skibbereen, in the North of Ireland, a very un- common custom exists which is known as " shrafting " the • word being a corruption of .shrove. On • Shrove , Tuesday a matrimonial " Tattersall "is held, when all the'", likely boys and girls "in the parish are on view, and all the marriages tor the ensuing year are made. For days there is astir in the neighbourhood, and the entire female population is in a flutter owing to the pre- parations for the gteat day. The" shrafting " is a pretty sight minuet', and if any wandering minstrel er artist came that way he might find a very taking subject for his pen or his brush. The • girls stand in a row on the village green, under the branch of a fine old copper' beech tree. At some little distance are gathered together a lot a shamed-faced looking men, all in their Sunday best,.and all looking as unconfortable and as foolish as they can. They have nothing active to do, their role is a passive one—to look at the girls while their mutual parents drive bargains, haggling and quarrelling about them as though they were so many beasts at a fair. Of course the young love will creep out here and there,but as a general thine the " boys and the " girls " ac- quiesce cheerfully in all the arrangementstliat are made on their behalf. There is one thing about this mode of getting a wife, and that is, it does not give either side much time to repent, except when the notices are deferred, until after Lest. It is probably this enforced leisure—no marriages are celebrated during Lent— which makes so many bridegrooms, when the fatal day arrives, appear "so late on the field. Punctuality on the part of the man is not a Strong plaint, and we have heard of a girl going with her friends, on three succes- sive Mornings before, the 'stating man toed the line. It is quite natural for 'to sympathise with the girl in these , circumstances; but *hot 'knovds'wbit conflicting emo- tions were wringing the dilatory grOoln'S bosom during those three days ? All this, of course, is mere sped don. As a rule, there is ' time for conflicting emotions, sin* both sides are usually in a hurry to visit his 'reverence, being content to let reflection follow leisurely in the train of the event. It happens now and again, a mime, that a young min may have , no kind friend or relative to make tsbargain for him ; and it is a by no means extraordinary thing for a young farm labourer so circumstanced to arrange .with the lady or her guardians and then find himself short of , the money for the priest's portion of the business, It once turned out, in an instance in which the girl, as well as her lover, was an orphan, •that the indispens- able coin could not be raised by either of the two, and the disconsolate fair one was met on the read by a sympathetic lady of the neighbourhood, sobbing as if her very heart would break. " Well, Mary, what's the matter ? Surely the boys cannot have passed you over? Never mind, better luck next time," said the lady. " Och, sure, it's not that at all, lady," replied Mary ; " I have me boy all settled. Sure„ it's Mickey Byrne, and a fine boy too. But neither of us has the half-crown to give his reverence, and we; eAn't be married till after harvest, and, ochi what. shill I do, what shall I do?" The lady whose Charity; was called upon in such a good cause as this, assurisrus that she could not resist the appeal. She adds that Mr. and Mrs. Byrne are now a thriving couple with a big farm and a growing family. Another point relative to Irish marriages is that matches are often made at wakes. This mixing up of the living with the dead is very singular, and to us it is revolting. There is something funny, however, in the case of the man whose second wife was found for him at the wake of his first.

div.head: 81IIP• CANAL.
div.p: THE 81IIP• CANAL.
--- ACCIDEN I' AT LATCHFORD.

A shocking accident befel a man named Win. Howell, employed on the Ship Canal, on Monday. Howell, who is a foreman mason, was working on a wall at Runcorn, when, owing to the slippery nature of the planks on which he was standing, he lost his footing, and falling to the kround, sustained a fractured rib and several other injuries. He was taken to the Latchford Hospital, where he now remains.

• OLDHAM COUNCIL AND THE SHIP CANAL. PROPOSED ADVANCE OF £250,000. On Wednesday evening a meeting of the Oldham rate- payers (the Mayor occupying the chair) was held at the Town Hall, when his Worship moved that the meeting consented to the Town Council promoting in the next Session of Parliament, at the expense of the borough fund, a, bill to obtain power* to enable the Corporation to advance £250,000 to the Ship Canal Company. Aid. Hall seconded the motion, which was carried by a large majority. Alderman Emmott, who heartily approved of the schema, then demanded a poll, which will take place on January 18th. CARGO SERVICE BETWEEN SALTPORT AND LONDON.

On Saturday afternoon * regular service of cargo steamers between the Ship Canal and London was Inau- gurated by the departure from Saltport of the steamship Lodore, 1,000 tons, belonging to the Manchester and LOndon Steam Shipping Company (Messrs. Fisher, Ren- wick, and Co., proprietors), and the following is a list of the first consignors and consignees :—Ermen and Bony, Patricroft ; Ermen and Roby, London ; Smithson Bros., Manebester ; Rylands and Sons, Limited,London ; Richard Hayworth, Manchester; Richard Hay- worth, London: W. Morley Gray, London; James Lewis and Co., Minchester • W. J. Davies and Son, Southwark; Lion Bros., London; G. Roakill and Co. Manchester; Pawson, Leaf, and Co., London; Baker and Brown, Manchester; W. H. Fertham and Co., London ; Hodder and Bullock. Pendleton; Galloways, Limited, Manchester ; Jean Dohmen Leblanc, Liege; Rayat, Antwerp; J. H. Gartside and Co., Manchester ; J. H. Gartside and Co., Limited, London; Arnati and Harrison, London; Armitage and Rigby, Manchester; Armitage and Rigby, London; J. T. Smith and J. E. Jones, Manchester; H. Comfort, London; Ed. Barlow, Manchester ; J.Wutting,London • Thomas de la hue and CO., London. A steamer left London at the same time for Saltport. We understand that a large number of applications have been received, and negotiations are in progress a such a nature as to give promise that a prosperous business will be rapidly developed. For the present the service will be weekly.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT STOCKTON HEATH. CENSURING THE COMPANY.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT STOCKTON HEATH. CENSURING THE COMPANY.

Mr. H. C.Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Latch- ford Hospital, on Tuesday, tguching the death of Frederick Caldwell, aged 13, who was killed on the Ship Canal at Stockton Heath, on Saturday, by being run over by a waggon, while foilowing his employment as a greaser or fatter. Mr. Percy Davies watched the case 6n behalf of the Ship Canal Company. Emma Caldwell sister of the deceased, said her brother had been employed on the Ship Canal about seven months. He went ti his work in good health on the morning in question, and some time later she heard that he had met with an accident. She went to the hospital at 12.30 and found that he was dead. On one occasion he had com- plained to her that the drivers of engines did not always give warning by whistling when coming up the line. James Gurney, rope runner, stated that he was on the engine " Timperley," on Saturday. There were eigh- teen waggons, fully loaded, attached to the engine. In front, on the same line, there was a number of waggons also fully loaded. When within some distance of these waggons, the driver of the " Timperley " stopped his engine, but the waggons behind " bumped up," and caused the engine to move and come in contact with the waggons in front. Witness then saw something move at the furthest end of the waggons in front, and

PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRITAING LO IrR STORY. BY LAURA JELIQ LIBBRY.
• CHAPTER XXXVL "I HAVE LEARNED ALL TOO LATE."
"'Did you throw yourself into the riverT I asked, In breathless horror.

"'No,' she arswered ; it was brought about by an accident. I fell into the water.' "'But there must have been someone about who heard your cries for help,' I exclaimed. '4 She buried her face in her hands and shook her head.
"The nest day that which I so mach dreaded happened. She spoke of leaving us, and wrote on to her friends that she was coming home..

"Only Heaven knows what I suffered that night: All through the long hours I paoed up and down under the light of the stars, crying out if she left us the happiness of life would be all over for me. "I knew full well that she could never love me, sir, for I was but a rough, ignorant man, and she was a dainty, lovely creature—just such an one as rich men choose for their brides. I could never give her silks and jewels and laces, nor coaches in which to ride. I could give her only an honest heart and a toil-hardened hand. Yes, yes, I realised full well that this dainty young girl was Rot for me; but I idolised her, as men idolise a golden star set in the blue heavens so far beyond their grasp. '"I will be strong enough and well enough to travel in a day or two,' she said, with a smile to mother. How glad you will be to be rid of your troublesome charge.' "Mother looked at me. She knew—oh, yes, she knew I—but she answered that she would be pleased if she could keep her there for ever. "'I am expecting a relative to come for me,' she said.
"And that afternoon a gentleman called. I passed him in the ball as he was leaving. One glance at his face, and I started back as though I had been shot.

"I had recognised in him a man whom I had been searching for for many a month. I was an eye-witness to a crime he committed one winter's night. "I will tell you how it happened, sir, and you will not wonder that I sought to save a young and lovely girl from such an atrocious fiend. "It was in Pittsburgh, one stormy night lan winter, sir, that it happened—the crime, I mean. "It was nearly midnight. I was hurrying along through the blinding storm and intense cold on an unfrequented road, when, suddenly, I stumbled and fell in the frozen path. I felt a sharp, horrible twiage of my left ankle, and when I tried to rise, I cried aloud with the intense pain of it. I realised In a moment what had happened. I had sprained my ankle.
Whether it was the intense cold or the intense pain that caused me to lose consciousness, I cannot tell. When I regained it, I found myself still lyirg where I had fallen, near a clump of bushes.

"And at that instant the sound of sharp, angry voices, in fierce altercation, fell upon my ears, and, struggling to my elbows, I saw two men standing scarcely twenty paces from me. I could see their faces clearly in the white, bright moonlight— though they could not see me, lying as I was in the dark shadows of the pines. "What the trouble was, I could not tell, but, as I looked, attempting to raise my voice to cry out to them for help, I save that which froze the sound on my lips. One of them had deliberately, and with- out warning, plunged a knife to the hilt in the other's breast.

"Every lineament Of the murderer's face stamped itself indelibly upon my brain; it is, the man who by this time, has wedded that innocent young girl. I would have faced him at the very altar and told my story. I was on my way to the church when fate prevented ma "Bat, bark you, sir I You have not heard the most atrocious part of the affair. Scarcely a moment had elapsed after the murderous blow was struck, ere footsteps were heard crunching the snow on the frozen path, and in an instant a man's form could be distinctly seen approaching. "The assassin wheeled ahont and sprang into a clump of bushes so near where I lay that I could have put out my band and touched him. Again I had a clear view of his face, as he watched the approach of the man coming quickly up the path. "'lt is he,' he muttered. 'Ha! a plan—worthy of the fiend himself—comes to me I I can—l—wsZi put it into execution.'

"He waited with breathless intensity the ap- proach of the other, as did I— to note what else might take place. " I could sec in the clear moonlight how unsteady the gait of the man coming up the icy path was; he had been imbibing too much wine. 'As I had expected, he stumbled over the body lying directly in his path, and an exclamation of intense dismay broke from his lips as he caught sight of the knife. In an instant he had drawn it forth—recognising, as he did so, with a cry of horror, the face of the dead.
" • lily enemy!' he gasped. Great God 1 Who has done this?' He did not see the serpent in human form who had crawled out from among the

"He did not know of his presence until he laid a heavy hand on his arm, exclaiming, while his evil face was aglow with satanic evil: " `Ah lam here in the nick of time,' he cried, 'to discover what you have done. I know you—l know the murdered matt. He was your friend, though you quarrelled bitterly in a down-town restaurant to-night. You vowed that you would kill him. You kept your vow.' "'Great God I ' cried the other, 'you do not mean tb say that /—/ have killed this man?' And he dropped • the knife in horror which he had clutched in his nerveless grasp. ." Precisely—l saw YOU,' repeated the scoundrel, deliberately. And as I live, sir, he actually talked the man into the belief that he had done the deed of which, Heaven knows, he was as innocent as a little babe. But when wine was in wit was out; be was actually talked into the infamous belief that he had committed the atrocious deed.

" I will not betray you. I would shield you,' said the rascal, smoothly. 'On one condition, and one condition only, will I consent to keep tour horrible secret and save you from the gallows. I will call and see you early to-morrow morning, and we will talk this matter over.' "You will wonder, sir, why I did not cry out and denounce the fiend incarnate when the foul lie was on his lips. I answer, in all candour, I dared not, for I was maimed and helpless; and if he had known that I witnessed the awful deed, there would have been two murders committed; he would have shown me no.roercy. Overcools with horror at the start- ling ,situatiou, I.roust have swooned again. When I returned to consciousness I was alone With the storm and the night. The two men bad gone. Even the victim had been removed and the white flakes which were beginnh,c; to fall from the now clouded sky were fast obliterating the traces of blood which had dyed the white snow." "'The villain has , escaped me,' was my first thought, but as sure as there is a living God I will hunt him down, that an innocent man whom he is making his dupe may not suffer for another crime. I hunted for him night and day, in crowded thoroughfares, in silent streets. I knew that I shnuld know him when we came lace to face, as I felt certain we should some time.

" And, sir, to make a long story short, the man whom I met coming from our house was the man whom I had witnessed commit the horrible crime. You will not wonder, then, that the next afternoon, when I heard he was wedded in a certain church at a certain hour to this fair young girl, I sought to save her; but I was too late. I would rather have seen lovely Miss Lawrence in—" Arthur Rochester sprang forward, white as death, as the name fell from Malcolm's lips. "What name was that I" he mied. "Speak it again—THE GIRL'S NAME r

As he had listened strange, wild fancies had thronged to his brain. His breath seemed to come from his lips in scorching, flaming fire. "What is the name of the girl whom you saved from the water six weeks ago? Speak quickly, man; do not torture me l"
, " Her name," replied Malcolm, "is bole Law- rence. She is, however, Miss Lawrence no longer, for, ere this, she has become the assassin's bride. Fate willed it so."
A bitter cry -Fell from Arthur Rochester's lips, as, in a glass, darkly, he could see the whole past out- lined before him.
" Oh, my God I—lonie rhe cried. "I know what has parted us—too late 1"
CHAPTER xxxvi. , 'SHE IS NOT HIS WIFE."
No pen can portray the poignant grief Arthur Rochester suffered as the awful truth burst upon him that the fair young girl, who had loved him so

well, had been fairly forced, through fraud, into marrying his rival. He clenched his strong hands together, and a bitter cry fell from his white lips. "It is too late to save her," he groaned; "but," springing to his feet in intense excitement, "I will follow them to the end of the world, and denounce him, and take her from him." Gaining from Malcolm explicit directions as to where the church was situated where the ceremony was to have been performed, Arthur set out for the place at once, in hopes of tracing from that point where they bad gone; but first, however, taking immediate steps to have young Malcolm's sanity clearly established, and his discharge accom- plished. It was a day's journey to his destination. Arthur Rochester never remembered how he reached it, his thoughts were in such a whirl. He found the old rector, who lived in an adjoin- ing cottage, at bogie. When he made known his errand the old gentleman looked at him hesitat- ingly. "You are a friend of the parties, sir 7" he in- quired. "Of the lady's," replied Arthar. "Then I will tell you what occurred, sirbb re- s turned the reverend gentleman, thoughtfully. "The ceremony which was to have made them one was commenced but never finished." "What l" cried Arthur, springing breathlessly for- ward. "Good heavens, sir do I hear aright—the ceremony was not concluded 7" "That is what I said," replied the minister. "If you will kindly give me your attention without. interruption f will relate briefly what occurred." Arthur had sunk back in his chair, trembling in every limb._
"I had been summoned rather hastily by the gentleman to pertains the eeremony as he wished to take the outgoing steamer for Europe that left that day, he said.

When r reached the church the bridal party, who hae preceded me, were already there. "In the course of my thirty years' experience I have seen many brides-elect, but never one like the one who stood before me. Her face looked like that of a dead woman's, pallid as marble, and her dark eyes fairly glowed like points of flame, and what caused me more surprise than all, the rest, was, she seemed to shrink from the very touch of the man whom she had come there to wed.

"Just before they reached the altar, she stopped short in the aisle and faced him, drawing herself up to her fullest height. "'Before this marriage takes place, I have one. request to make of you,' she said. "Consider it granted beforehand, if it is in nyr
power," he replied. "She drew from the. pocket of her dress a foldea

paper and placed it in his hands. " • Read that over carefully,' she said. Then it. Is my request that you sign it and return it to u..c ere the ceremony shall proceed.' "He glaliced over the paper hurriedly, then— Heaven forg!ve me for the remark—but his faca grew actually fiendish. '"I absolutely refuse to sign that!' he exclaimed. angrily. • Yon might have known I would obieet to such an arrangement. Leave you to go your wsv after the ceremony, and Igo mine, indeed ! ' And as he spoke he tore the paper into shreds and eas,, them on the floor. -'I am not a man to be trifled. with in, this fashion,' be went on, storrni:y. 'Either the marriage takes place here and now. i;r It does not. Understand, there is no coercion. Ent you know what will occur in case you do not rvtain with me as my wife.'

"` Let the sacrifice go on, if it must,' she' answered. " Sir,' said I stepping forward 'you pardon me. From what I see and boar Infer that this marriage would be distasteful to the lady, and, under the circumstances, I cc.nfrt rot thiak of performing the ceremony, I assure you.' "She turned tome and I shall never for-st, the

hunted look in the darkly beautiful eyes. " 'Oh I good sir, the marriage must go on!' Si cried. beg you to reconsider what you havo said. Do not heed what has transpired. Think of it only as a young girl's unreasonable whim?, " ' Since you really desire it, I will perform lit' ceremony with pleasure,' I declared, heartily, isatco relieved at this phase of affairs. " Silently they took their places before me, ana Clearly and distinctly the beautiful marriage F-ervice was read to them. The gentleman made his restiot firmly and distinctly; then I turned to the fair young girl, noticing she had grown paler, if 03' were possible, than before.

"Vilt thou take this man to be thy la wfully wedded husband, to love, honour, cherish anti obey,' I asked, solemnly, 'until death do you part "She turned those great humid eyes upon me, and a bitter cry fell from her white lips. " I cannot bind myself by a false oath,' eh° cried; I cannot say I will love, honour, and obey this man whom I abhor. Heaven help me! I can- not say it l' And with these words she threw up her white arms and fell at the would. be bricieroord+ fe.or in dnpn svv non "I was almost paralysed by the bitter curses twit fell from the man's lips, and in that holy place. "Pronounce this lady ray wife," he said, imps' tiently, 'that we may be gone.' "This, I assured him, indignantly, was not to be thought of. st:n.dls can forcelaainmy choeurrtaso fmlayww; f he jt he cried. do the . affair "Not until you are pronounced man and wife,' I replied, firmly, bidding him raise her while I went to the house for ice-water and assistance. "I could not have been gone five minutes, Sir, When I returned the would-be bridegroom and the lovely young girl were gone "The two people whom they had brought with them to witness the ceremony said that immedi- ately upon my leaving them, he had raised the giri quickly in his arms, and without one word et explanation had rushed from the church with his fair burden, placed her in a coach, and the driver had dashed down the road at a hreakeeeh pace. " That is the last I have seen or heard of them, and I confess I have spent very many anio,l:,: moments wondering if they went to some clergyman for for the purpose of having the ccreraon:: performed, or whether he dared carry oat his threat, of claiming her." a "If he has, he shall settle with ma for it!" C`'e Arthur Rochester, who had listened with brcathle* intensity to the minister's story. Half an hour later he was on his way to Ne'v seaWrbhherefbrinbisthdisarliwbigd,e,towiwdreest worldher York city, his heart and brain in a whirl. assassin's power ?" he cried out to himself, in powerless ITHth e 0, occurred whot ow thoughtao iudlwtdoba have rah:: terrible agony nmea dhg4rvhbeati manner in which to discover their whereabouts was to engage the service of an experienced detective. When he reached the city Arthur drove at once to the main bureau of the agency. He found the chief in, and was conducted at onbce to the private office, despite the gilt letters on t gla.ss door to the effect that admission was strictlY prohibited. nintn aghetitshooeflhi need.fixnem of. so tr Wfler 0 x° nl'apilNbe tills a st The chief glanced up, and seeing a tall, handsorne gentleman standing before him, motioned him to a seat. "I shall be at leisure in a very few momenta," the chief, turning to the batch of letters which had come in by the noon mail, and sorting them rapidly, "then I shall attend you with pleasure." Arthur bowed and took the proffered seat. Although seeming ' ly intent upon the perusal of his letters, the chief had spent ten minutes or more in watching the thoughtful, averted face of hi visitor. It was an old habit with him, and in mail s instances had proved of valuable service to him. He turned to Arthur at length, and signified tlrt he was "ready to hear what he had to say now.' "I have called to see you in reference to ii' young lady," said Arthur, stopping short in em- barrassment. The chief smiled under his thick moustache. „ "No doubt it was some entangling. love affair' he concluded; and he wondered why men came to him to extricate them from their j difficulties. In all probability he had fallen los with some little beauty, and a stern papa I' smuggled her off and had hidden her securely sonl,l, where. It was surprising how many youeg came to the bureau to seek their aid in searchict for their sweethearts. As in duty bound, be look profoundly interested. The thrilling narrative Arthur told him awakened the keenest interest of the chief. thia;, "The mysterions murder in Pittsburgh on. winter's night which you refer to, I remember wti,le he said, "for I happened to he in that city at time. No clue was ever found to the perPetrl'ut°r- So this is the man who has inveigled this girl into marrying him. I will assure you of t —no time shall be lest in tracking the 011°. down."

div.p: SANKEY SCHOOL 'HOARD AND FitEE EDUCATION. A meeting of the Great Sankey School 8,, rd was held at the Clerk's office, Bewsey-st., Warrington, on Tuesday forenoon, Captain Ridgway in the chair. The other members present were—Mr. W. P. Skelton (vice-chairman), Mr. Joseph Wright, Mr. Samuel Sutton (clerk), and Mr. George Clarke (achoolmaster) 1

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL REPORT.

The Cmattx read the annual ten-Mit—of the Government Inspector, which was as followS:—" Mixed, school : Discipline is well maintained. and the work, taken as a whole, and considering the quite recent disturbance of, the school by sickness. is ef good merit. The papers are neatly done, with good penmanship and tieuring. spell- ing is satislfactory, and written arithmetic is efficient in the first four standards, but composition and written arithmetic (especially the latter) need attention in the sth and ffih standards, with reading in the Ist standard. The class subjects, except as regards hemming in the 2nd standard, are very successfully prepared, as also are recitation and singing by. note." "Infants' class: The infants are orderly, And do their work as well as Gould be expected considering all circumstances. More attention should, however, be given to the mental arith- metic, and a better general impression made by ttie ebject lessoas.°—The CHAIRMAN thought the report was rather favourable.—Mr. CLAIMER : Under the new system of fee grant we make £ll instead of losing at all.

div.head: A.URQUEST POR FRIA MACES,
div.p: A.URQUEST POR FRIA MACES,

The Clerk said a letter had been received from one whe was evidently anxious to shine as an amateur poli- tician, and who wished to teach the members of the bard their duties. The letter was as follows:—" 53. Chapel-road. Penketh, November 27. Mr. Clerk. Dear Sir,—l have sent my children to school this week with- out their school pence, and the reason I have done so is not that I cannot afford to pay it ; it is through the correspondence I have read this week on the sub- ject. I enclose you Mr. Acland's reply to Hyde, also his remarks. If the Act of Parliament gives us a Free Edu- cation Bill, every workingman has a perfect right to have the full benefit of the said Act. As it is carried out at the present moment it is neither one thing nor the other. Some one must take steps in the matter, so I come forward in this district to test the matter. The school managers, who, either in ignorance or with intent to mislead, convey an entirely wrong imprea- lion respecting free education. Let me charitably hope it is the former. The subject is of such vast importance to the working class, and indeed the public generally, that I need not apolog ze for drawing your particular attention to it. I should feel obliged if you would place it before the Board.—t am, yours respect- , fully, JOHN RODGERS." The Clerk said the reference to Mr. Acland was as follows :—Mr. Acland has addressed the following letter to Mr. 'I homes Proetor,of Gee Cross, Hyde, who wrote to him complaining that he and other parents in the district are unable to obtain free school places for their children without going through an "ordeal of pauperism," and that they still have to pay fees in spite of having made representations to the De- partment :—" Education Department, November 18, 1 1892. Dear Sir,—The Department are taking action to secure the provision of the free school places claimed by you and other parents. But the means of doing so provided by the Act of 1891 necessarily involtte some delay where the demand for free places is not met bv voluntary local action. I have read with surprise and regret the printed circular issued from Hyde British School, and bearing upon it the names of the managers. It is tie astonishing thing that such a eircular, issued on the 11th of last month, should contain these words. ' there is no such thing as free education,' and should add that upon proof of poor circumstances' a. remission of fees will no doubt be obtained. It can- not be too clearly and widely understood that under the Act any and every parent in England and Wales, irres- pective of any question as to his means, is entitled to claim completely free education for his children, and that it is the statutory duty of the Department to see that free education is provided accordingly. 1 would further empress the hope that all local scheol authorities, whether school boards or voluntary managers, will co-operate loyally in ca rrying out the intentions of Parliament, and will not make any ill-advised attempt to use the Act so as to raise distinctions of wealth and class, or to attach invidous conditions to the acceptance of its benefits. Such action if taken on any considerable scale must inevitable result in fresh legislation, with the concurr- once of both political parties, making such a publication as the circular you enclose an impossibility.—Yours faithfully, A. 11. D. ACLAND. Mr. T. Proctor."—The circular alluded to above was as follows :—" Dear Sir,— Your child has come to school without the fees which are necessary. There is no such thing, as free education. The new Act of Parliament only provides for paying part of the fees in this school. If, however, you appeal to the managers and prove to them that poor circumstances make the payment of fees a hardship, they will no doubt remit the other half of the fees, but until. you have done this the fees must be paid.—Yours, WIC GIBSON. Managers :—The Rev. H. E. Howson, Alderman E. Hib- bed, Councillor A. T. flibbert."— Mr. 'SUTTON added that he had been informed by the schoolmaster that the children did not live in the district ; it was, however, a qquestion whether it would be policy to adopt the stan- dard. He also read another letter from Mr. Rodgers, who said :—" My daughter tells me you say I am not in the district. This a fact lam perfectly aware of, and I want the Board to clearly understand that lam not tak- ing these measures for :ny own benefit alone ; it is for the public at large. If the Act of Parliament gives us a a free Bill, as Mi. /inland says, why keep it from us P"— The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Rodgers lives in Penketh P—The Canni: Yes, sir.—The Quitman : Has he tried the question on at Penketh F—T e CLERK replied in the negative.—The CHAIRMAN: Why does he try it on at Sankey then 2—Mr. CLAMED : Because he sends his chil- dren to us. Mr. SRZLTON : What is Mr. Rod- pts ? Mr. amiss : He is in the service of Mr. Garnett. He chooses our school because he thinks the children will have the best education.— Mr.Skeiton : Are we to be dictated to by a man who Is neither a ratepayer nor a resident ? That is the question we have to discuss to-day. If we take Mr. Rodger's children we may take others from Manchester, Liverpool, and elsewhere..—The Clerk: I think the circular ot the Hyde people is an error. A free school is bound to provide free places. leis a question whether we are bound to provide them for Penketh, seeing that there is a school there. I have looked the question up, and I find the 86001 district is alluded to. We are bound to find places for children in the district— not for those living in another district where a school is provided.—The Chairman : I take it that Mr: Rodgers has to apply to Penketh first,and if there is no accomo- dation there it becomes a question whether he must not go to the nearest school.—The Clerk: That is my opinion ; hut it is a matter of policy. We have but a small percentage of children from Sankey, and we have to look to the lee erant.—Mr. Skelton : Would it not be policy, not to allow people to think he had forced our band—to make the school completely free 2 We have plenty of room, and it is proved by the action we adopted last year that we are more in pocket than we otherwise should have been —The !;lerk : I was going to suggest, without recognizing this man's right to dictate to you,or even to suggest,because he is out of the district that it would be wise under the circumstances to give the matter a month's trial, until the next meeting, and grant free places to those who seek them.—The Chair- man : If you once begin you must go on. It is a question whether we must make the school free, or tell this man to apply to Penketh.—Mr. SKELTON : The thing lies in a nutshell. All we should loso by abolishing the school fees we should gain by having an increased Government grant.—Mr. CLARKS : If any child in the district applies for tree education we are bound to provide it, that is clear.—Mr. SKELTON : Yes, but I should like it to be understood that we have the power to rectum children from outside the district.—The CLERK :If there is no school within miles you are bound to take the children, but there is such a school In the township to which this man's children have a tight to go, and in which township, I presume, he is a ratepayer.—Mr. Sminron proposal that the further con- sideration of the matter be adjourned to the next meet- ing, and that in the meantime Mr. `3larke be instructed to refuse all children residing outside the township of Great Sankey, appearing without the school pence from Standard four udwards.—The motion was seconded by Mr. Wiliam, and carried.
ST. HELENS MINERS AND THE FOREST OF DEAN REDUCTION.,,

At a meeting of miners at St. Helens, on Satur- day. the questions of organisation and the position of the Forest of Dean miners, N% ho are threatened I with a reduction of 7i per cent., were considered. Air. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, felt assured that next summer would bring to the test the question whether the employers or the Miners Federation of Great Britain were the strongest. He urged the miners to save one or two shillings per week, and be prepared to fight nobly and loyally. Their powerful federation had already prevented a reduction of the wages of those , isetesent, and they had better support the Forest of Dean,l and nip in the bud attempts to reduce wages.—Mr.. ' lkl'lcinley, chairman, said St. Helens bail always joined forward mevernents for the benefit of miners generally. --Resolutions pledging the members to exert themselves to get all the men and boys about the collieries to join ' the organisation, and support the forest of Dean either by subscriptions or, along with the whole of the Fede- ration of Great Britain, laying down their tools, were ,carried unanimously.

div.head: W ARRIN GTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: W ARRIN GTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Greenell) in.the chair, the deputy-mayor (Alderman Francomb), Aldermen Holmes, Sutton. Wright; an i Blackhurst ; Councillors Fleming, Wilkinson, Hepherd, Hutchinson, K. T Faircloigh, Monks, Shaw Green, Plumpton. Muir, Roberts, Greening, Hill, Browne, Beaman, Smethurst, Shaw, Ashton. Bonneli. Dixon. Bolton, Tinsley • Mr.J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer, and Mr. Longdin. Borough Surveyor.

div.head: WATCH COMMITTEE.
div.p: WATCH COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended :—That the following members be appointed the Visiting Committee of the Bridewell :—Aldermen Francomb and Sutton ; and Councillors Cannel! (convener), and Heaton. That the folloWing members be appointed a Sub-Committee to inapset the report upon all places licensed for the per- formance of stage plays :—Aldermen Chandley and Francomb ; Councillors Carmen, Fleming, and Heaton (convener). That a licence be granted to Mr. Sylvanus Reynolds for the performance of stage plays, at the Latchford Parish Room, for 12 months from this date, subject to the usual conditions upon which such licenses were formerly granted by the Justices. The Mama proposed the adoption. Alderman FBA:moms seconded, and the report was adopted. HEALTH COMMITTEE.—THE EPIDEMIC.

This Committee recommended : That the tender of Messrs. Manlove. Alliott, and Company, Limited, for the supply for a Washington Lyon's patent steam disinfector at £282, and that of the Grantham Crank and Iron Co., Limited, to supply a vertical boiler, 8 h.p., for £45, be accepted. The Committee's report contained a number of recommendations for defiling with the epidemic by Dr. F. W. Thomson, one of the medical officers to the Local Government Board, which we have already pub- d.—The Committee recommended : That the Town Clerk give notice to the Newton Improvement Commis- sioners to terminate the agreement of April 25th, 18S8, for the reception of patients from hewton into the Infectious Diseases Hospital at Warrington. Alderman Stirrott proposed the adoption of the minutes. He remarked as to the recommendation to accept Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co's tender for the supply of a disinfector that the disinfector in use at Aikin-st. Hospital being insufficient to meet the increased require- ments brought about by the outbreak of small-pox, the Committee were compelled to get an additional one without delay. The one ordered disinfected by mettns of steam instead of hot air,and did its work most effectually. Thee had learned that there was a similar machine at Tottenham, and on a recent visit there by him, the medical officer in charge of the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital there told him he had had a good deal of experi- ence, and he considered it the best extant, and that no failure could possibly happen in its working. Alderman Sutton then referred to the Committee's recommenda- tion of the acceptance of the tender of the Grantham Crank and Iron Company for a boiler. This boiler, he said, was used in connection with the disinfector. With reference to the small-pox epidemic it would be observed that Dr. T. W. Thomson, one of the medical inspectors for the Local Government Board, had visited Warrington, and made four recommendations in respect to the epidemic. The Committee, being fully alive to the serious character of the epidemic, which at that time continued to get worse, lost no time in endeavouring to carry out the recommendations. The first recommenda- tion was that further accomodation for the isolation of per- sons suffering from smallpox should at once be provided at a distance of a mile from any village or other centre of population ; and a sub-committee was appointed to visit all likely sites in the neighbourhood for the purpose of finding one which, as far as possible, would meet the views of the Local Government Board, as exnressed by Dr. Thomson. The sub-committee, however, found that such a site within a reasonable distance from Warring- ton was not to be obtained se easily as might be imagined, and they partly came to the conclusion that in the event of any other more suitable site not being available they should obtain the consent of the Gas and Water Committee to make use of the land connected with a farm at Orford belonging to the Corporation for a temporary hospital, in case the disease should continue to increase. In order to be prepared for an emergency such as was then expected, Dr. Gornall and he went to London, where they had further consultation with Dr. Thomson, and went on to Tottenham to inspect the buildings in use at the infectious diseases hospital there, in order to obtain information. The fourth recom- mendation of Dr. Thomson appeared to be a most important one, and related to vaccination and re-vac- cination, and being backed up later on by a resolution of the medical profession in Warrington, was promptly carried out, as would be seen by the resolution that the medical officer be empowered to establish stations for gratuitous vaccination, and the live medical gentlemen appointed attendee every night for about a fortnight at the five stations in the differ- ent wards of the borough. It was admitted that not fewer than 1,800 persons presented themselves to be vaccinated and re-vaccinated at these stations. During the last week, applications for vaccination had been very much fewer, and the Committee thought it neces- sary under the circumstances to give notice that these vaccination stations wwld be discontinued; and that notice had been accordingly given. The Committee be- lieved that their prompt and decisive action, aided by the Medical Officer of Health, and the various other members of the medical profession in Warrington, had had some effect in arresting the progress of the infection, and although the decrease in the number of multiplied cases was not equal to the expectations of a week ago, hopes were still entertained that the effects of vaccina- tion of such a large number of persons in the town—it was calculated that at least 12,000 persons had been vaccinated altogether—must bring about a material diminution in the number of cases, and that it might not now be necessary to provide an additional tempor- ary hospital the provision of which would be attended with a cost of many thousands of pounds. But it was thought that at some early date arrangements might be made either solely or in oe,iniunction with some adjoining town—(cries of" Hear, hear ")—to provide a perman- ent hospital in some convenient locality. Greet credit, he thought, was due to the principals at Dallam and 13ewsey ironworks, and other works in the town, for the encouragement they had given to the working men in their employ to become vaccinated ; and it was some- what satisfactory to know that many hundreds of persons in their employment cheerfully came forward, and acceded to the request made to them. Alderman Sutton said he should conclude by saying that he thought they had sufficiently proved that vac- cination was a most important element in arresting smallpox, and he believed it was the opinion of most medical men that the reason why smallpox had occur- red in so many different towns was principally the fact that of late years very strenuous and increased opposi- tion had been given to vaccination in all parts of the country, and the public became negligent, or altogether refused to support vaccination. Alderman Sutton re- ferred to a minute of the committee declining to receive any further patients from Newton district,and stated ,that as the Town Clerk had intimated that the Local Govern- ment Board considered it necessary that the hospital should be Properly isolated, the Corporation could not very well continue to receive patients from other places, hence notice had to be given to that effect to the New- ton Improvement Commissioners. Alderman BLACIEHURST seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor HILT. asked if any time had been given to the people of Newton to prepare a place of their own. The Mavon : Three months. Alderman FHANCOME asked if Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co., Limited, had the sole right to manufacture the steam disinfectors, and if not, whether a Warrington tradesman had had a chance of competing. Alderman SUTTON : Yes, they have the sole right. Councillitr R. T. Autumn thanked the Medical Officer for putting a mapup in the hall showing the course taken by smallpoz,but said it might be improved if they had statistics so that they could trace the disease from the commencement. It would be much better if the Health Committee could give them charts of the disease throughout the town instead of a mass of figures. Councillor BONNELL expressed his regret that Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co. had the monopoly of the dis- infector, as but for that fsct one could have been ob- tained chenier. Councillor DIXON: I should be very glad if the Cor- poration would have Wilderspool Causeway kept clean. The MAYOR: Nothing to do with the Health Commit- tee.

Councillor BEAMAN said the patent of the steam dis- infector was not that of the Arm mentioned, but that of a Mr. Washington Lyon : but Messrs. Manlove, Alliott. and Co., had the sole right of manufacture. It would do in 20 minutes what one of their obsolete disinfeltors would do in eight hours. Councillor HUTCHINSON complained of delay in disin- fecting houses from which smallpox patients had been removed. Alderman Surrox requested him to name a case. Councillor Hu'rcumsoN said he could, but had been advised not to do so. Alderman SUTTON Put it in writing. Councillor Iltyrcanotm said be would bring the matter before the Chairman of the Committee. Councillor Mune said he was informed, and Dr. Ger- nail said the other night in the Health Committee—and what he said was substantiated by Mr. Norman—that

I alinast immediately after a patient was removed from a I house it was fumigated. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH : A very proper answer (Laughter.) Councillor Huvenneisosi : , A. far as you know. , Alderman Sorrow said the Committee hid had to do with Wilderspool-road, but they had prictically_handed it over to the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and he had no doubt it would be attended to by that Committee. In regard to the observations of Councillor Hutchinson, he could not understand why these complaints were being continually brought forward. The Health Com- mittee were continually inquiring on the , subject, and the reply was that every house had been attended to without delay. It seemed to him that people talked and I made complaints just' for the sake of talk. He had no hesitation in saying that when the Committee ;came to examine Into any case a laid before) them by Councillor Hutchinson. they would find them to be on a par with all the rest of the statements made—to have nothing in them. He ceuld promise Mr. Hutchinson that if there were any justification for his complaint, the Committee would tikes great care that all cause of complaint was obviated in future. SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE. .The minutes of this Committee contained the appoint- ment of a Longford Sub-Committee consisting of the following, gentlemen :—The Chairman, Deputy Chair- Man (Convener) and Councillors Bonne% Dixon Green- ing, and Smethurst; and horses and stables sub-commit- tee, Councillors Dixon, Smethurst, and Roberts. It was also decided to connect the Longford and Howley depits by telephone. Councillor MONKS, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, said that the machinery at Longford was in a very efficient state' and well able to deal with the material. Indeed the works had occasionally to wait eight and sometimes sixteen hours a week for material, so far ahead did they get with the work. Councillor Bealiax in seconding the adoption said that probably at the next meeting they would be able to set something before the Council in connection with the works, which would be in the nature of a revelation to them. ("Oh, oh," and laughter.) The minutes were adopted. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The following gentlemen were appointed as a Sub- Committee: The Chairman, Deputy Chairman, and Councillors Ashton, Flood, and Hutchinson. The minutes contained a resolution to the effect that a plot of land in Cartwright-st., consisting of 956 acres, be leased to Mr. George Wallington at a ground rent of £6 10s. per annum. In moving the adoption of the minutes Alderman Wright alluded to this resolution,and raid they were bringing to a conclusion what had been a very disagreeable matter, which had been left to them as a legacy, namely a law suit. They were about to lease the plot tor land to Mr. Wallington at Le 10s. per aanum. They would have to pay a certain sum to the original landowner, but he considered they would come out of the matter without loss if the remainder of the land were let satisfactorily. He also mentioned that the, had had a grant of £453 from the County Council for the main- tenance of "secondary roads.' Councillor.R. T. FAIRCLOUGH seconded the adoption. Councillor Furman] wished to make a complaint about the dangerous condition of grids on the footpath. He alluded to two occasions on the previous day, when he had narrow escapes from falling in Buttermarket-street, and then he mentioned that at night he slipped on one that was concealed in the snow, and fall to the ground. (Laughter.) Councillor SUTTON: What tune at night was it when you fell? (Loud laughter.) Councillor FLEMING : Well, it didn't happen to be later than six o'cleek. Alderman Sutton is inclined to "chaff "me, Mr. Mayor. (Laughter.) Con uing, the speaker said that owners of property sho4ld be com- pelled to keep those grids in proper order, and he thought the Council ought to see to it. e Councillor FROWNS alluded to the flooding of , Mersey-street, opposite the Post Office. He said the I road was constantly in a filthy state owing to the flooding if the drains, and the health of the inhabitants was constantly endangered. Councillor Smiw referred to the insanitary condition of certain streets in St. John's Ward. They were old streets/ and if the chairman of the committee could see his way to pay attention to them be should be pleased. Councillor Dixon called attention to certain houses in Padgate-lene which should have sewers laid to them. Councillor Ptusirrox again complained of the condi- tit!' of the passage between Leicester-at. and Elizabeth- et.. which was, he said, in a most disgraceful condition. There were 30 or 40 tenants in the housed, and the pas- sage was in such a condition that they could not get out of their back doors. Alderman WRIGHT said with regard to Councillor Browne's complaint, that storm overflow pipes had been ordered, and the committees were waiting for them. The question of the paving of Mersey-st. should be inquired into. The streets alluded to by Councillor Shaw should be attended to; the contracts would be out in a short tinte. He did not wonder at Councillor Plump- ton's complaint, as the work should have been done long since. If the contractor did not do it forthwith someone else should take it up. The sub-committee had been to Padgate-lana, and they expected a report on Monday week. The minutes were then passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that the average attendance at the public elementary schools (hiring the month of October was 8,101 ; corresponding period last year, 8,237 ; decrease, 136. Councillor Ftemixo moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee, and in doing so he commented on the remarkably small number of absentees under the exist- ing circumstances. In spite of that fact, however, the committee had the greatest difficulty in prevailing sin parents to insist on their children going to school. Some were so frightened that they positively defied the com- mittee. Under the circumstances the committee deemed it advisable not to press the cases against the defaulters too harshly, hoping that before a lapse of many weeks the scare having passed away, there would be the normal attendances. The school teachers were complain- Mg very much of the decrease in the school fees conse- quent on the absence of children, but he was afraid that the committee were powerless to help them at the present juncture. Councillor Swim-Glum; seconded the adoption of the minutes,and in doing so he said that if the Council were desirous of being informed en what grounds the com- mittee had not closed the schools, he would refer them to Dr. Gornall's report,which was published the previous week. Be had expected that the decrease would have been much larger than it was. Couucillor Mosors suggested that as the attendances were so unsatisfactory to the school teachers from a financial point of view, the schools had better be closed. (" No, no.") In the event of the schools being closed the managers of them would receive a Government grant, which they alleged they would lose if the present state of affairs continued. After further d'scussion the minutes were adopted. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, ARTS, AND TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION 'COMMITTEE. Greening (convener), F. W. Monks, Peers, and Roberts. The thanks of the meeting were forwarded to the donors of the following gifts:—" Priory Church of 'Fynemouth,"

' Councillor BROWNE desired to be informed whether the Committee had any intention of prohibitingithe holding of horse fairs in the public streets. Councillor Roßairrs remarked that it appeared to him to bee foolish thing on the part of the committee to allow of the congregation of such large crowds at the pleasure fair, when the Corporation were expending such large sums of money in precautionary measures to stamp out the smallpox epidemic. Continuing, he sug- gested the desirability of abolishing the fair. WATER COIEMITTEE.-APPLETON WATER.

The managing sob-committee of the Corporation con- sists of the following gentlemen :—The Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, and Messrs. Shaw-Green, Efepherd, and Roberts. The report of the county analyst on a sample of the Appleton water (filtered) appeared in Saturday's Examiner. It stated that the sample con- tained a considerable quantity of organic matter of vegetable origin, but contained nothing of the nature of sewage. It was suitable for domestic use. Alderman FRAWCOME proposed the adoption of the minutes, and in doing so he referred to the result of the analysis which had been made by the County Analyst. Be assured the Council that although the water had been certified to be fit for domestic purposes, the committee did not intend to use it, inasmuch as there was an abundance of water at Winwick to satisfy all the de- mands of Warrington for some time to come in regard to domestic use. The committee had been given to un- derstand that the presence of the organic matter in the water was due to the incapacity of the filter beds, but if ever the occasion arose for the necessity of tappin,s, the water for domestic purposes the Council might rest assured that every, precaution would be taken in respect to filter beds.
Grunsillor FLamnse seconded the adoption of the ml flutes.

Councillor BOLTON thought that the County Analyst meant.the Council to understand that the expression for domestic purpOses was meant to imply only fit for washing purposes. The Councillor then proceeded to attack the correctness of the analysis as showing the water being fit for domestic use on account of the large proportion of nitrogen and the presence of other mat- ters in suspension. He was surprised, he said, to find that the County Analyst had attached his name to such a result as was laid before them.

Councillor Romears remarked that it was hardly to be expected that Councillor Bolton would put his certificate to any class Df water. (Laughter.) He had suggested that Dr. Campbell Brown was only a second rate autho- rity, and he (Councillor Roberts) would suggest that before the Water Committee attempted to use the water in question they would apply to the greatest authority on the subject—Councillor Bolton. (Laughter.) Several references were then made to the insufficient pressure at the water mains on the occasion of a fire in Folly-lane. Alderman rRANCOVB. in replying, said the Committee were doing their best to compete with the work, but it was impossible for them to cover the town with ade- quate mains within twelve months. With respect to the bad supply of water at fires, he could only suggest to the peoole in the neighbourhood of Folly-lane, te try and do without having their houses on fire for a time, because they did not stand in any immediate prospect of having the force of water increased, just yet. (Laughter.) The minutes were then carried.
