div.head: ANTI-VACCINISTS' CASE.
div.p: THE ANTI-VACCINISTS' CASE.
BY AN ANTI-VACCINATOR.

In reading reports of vaccination prosecutions, and of discussions among the members of Boards of Guardians on cases of vaccination defaulters, the casual reader is, as a rule, led to infer that these recusants are exceedingly stupid and ignorant people—mere cranks, crotchetmongers and faddists. and are actuated in their opposition to the law solely by prejudice. It is indeed commonly im- plied by magistrates, and others in authority, that these recusants have no case whatever. And yet it must be obvious to all who intelligently and can- didly consider this question that the anti-vaccinists have a strong case ; so strong indeed is it that it has impressed with its strength some of the acutest and best trained minds in Europe. The simple fact is that what Carlyle termed " swarmery," and Johnson "illusion" has completely deluded the public in this matter. A tradition has been handed down : it has been incorporated into a law :it has called into existence a class of officials who live by it wholly or in part, and the result is a foregone conclusion. _

Smallpox as a disease has been so to speak, vio- lently wrenched from its natural position both in national and in medical history. It has been dealt with as if it were something quite different in effect and apart from other xymotic diseases ; and the view has in effect been ignorantly taught and as ignorantly accepted that it will never (unlike the plague, the black death, the sweating sickness, leprosy and scurvy) die out of itself, but will always be present, and always need the presence of a small army of special officials, vaccinators, Stc., to deal with it specially. Needless to say the case of the antivaccinists is I the reverse of this. They believe, on the contrary, that diseases decrease and die out, as they arise and increase, by natural causes ; and they see no reason why smallpox should prove an exception. Hence they join issue with the most fundamental pro- positions of their opponents. When it is urged that smalluox was of old a scourge, they reply that there is a good dPal of exaggeration about the matter, as in the worst smallpox period in London (in the 18th century) when the disease was at its highest (thanks tn., the medical wiseacres of that time who encouraged smallpox inoculation) not 4,000 deaths occurred there in any one year, while in the lowest year of that century but 522 died from it. And. they point to the statement of Dr. Wm. Farr, for 40 years the highest statistical authority in Eng- land, who says of London in his "Vital Statistics," that smallpox, with fever, was declining before vaccination was discovered, indicating as he says the general improvement in the public health then taking place. It was a mere coincidence they urge, that vaccination was introduced at a juncture, when owing to improved modes of living, caused by the birth of the new sanitary science, human life be- came more valuable. The terms " swarmery • and "illusion" have been used. To illustrate what is meant by them it may be said that so far back as the year 1825 and subsequently, the official reports of the National Vaccine Instituiion in London used precisely the same gratulations that are made use of to-day by many self-deceived honest people. At that time but the merest fraction of the population were vaccinated; and yet we find these vaccination zealots rejoioing over the alleged but altogether baseless discovery, that then, thanks to vaccina- tion, it was rare to find a pock-marked person at a theatre or other place of public entertainment! , Thus did imagination—as it still does—run away with the commonsense and judgment of interested or credulous people. These people did not see, nor do their intellectual successors now see, that even granting the truth of their allegation, yet this vac- cination would not acconnt for the equally great decline in the mortality from fever. Nor would it account for the still greater decline, or the total disappearance of the other malignant diseases re- ferred to above.

The anti-vaccinists, supported by Chadwick and , all deep thinking hygienists, asserts that to BM human life, to affect the general total death-rata-- for to attack one disease of this group while leav- ing the general conditions unaltered is but to leave mom for a similar disease to step in—the whole group of such diseases must be aimed at ; otherwise the gain is much like the Irishman's in cutting off a piece from the bottom of his blanket to sew it on at the top. This view coneantly commended itself to the venerable and veteran Chadwick, whose knowledge of such subjects was vast and profound. Anti-vaccinists can smile at their puny critics fortified, as they are, by Chadwick's authority. They deny, too, the validity of the official tables as to the relative mortality from smallpox of vac- cinated and unvaccinated patients. Of the former class the mortality is put at one per cent. and even lest; of the latter class the mortality is (officially) said to range from 35 to DOper cent. Anti-vaccin- ists pertinently enough ask, in view of the fact that the disease is the same new as of old, why the unvaccinated now die in these days of improved medicine at this heavy rate,. when it is conchisively established that before vaccination was invented the average fatality from smallpox was about 18 per cent, of cases ? And they further point to the fact established bofore the present Royal Commis- sion, that calculating without regard to the " marks" theory, the average fatality-rate from smallpox is almost exactly the same now as it was in those pre-vacnine days I Hence they naturally brand the" marks theory as a delusion or.a fraud.

Nor can they accept the orthodox and official state- ments as to the alleged harmlessness of vaccination. Not only is one death per week from vaccination registered in England, but there are very good grounds for believing that these deaths form but a very small portion of those caused by vaccination, but which are huddled out of sight by the mislead- ing medical certificates given "in order to preserve vaccination from reproach." " The alleged evil con- sequences of vaccination says Governmental cir- culars issued throughout the land by local bodies, "are contrary to all medical experience." But anti- vaccintists point out that, setting aside indepen- dent inquirers, official evidence has been in the possession of the Government since 1807, refuting such gross mis-statements. In that year the Royal College of surgeons, in response to a Government request, prepared and presented a report, compiled

cal adviser to the Government, in his--" "Papers oi vaccination" presented to Parliament just 50 years later (1857). On this point they would quote the substance of some conclusions come to by the I.a- -penal German Commission on vaccination in 18E4 —a body some five-sixths pro-vaccinists. They say that " There are real and serious dangers incidental to vaccination," that " erysiphelas and other in- jurious consequencss, are by no means uncommon," that the possibility of t'de invaccination of syphites is incontestable," and that the prevalence of scrofula in the population renders it unsafe to use children as vaccinifers.° It may be added that in the pre- vious year the London Makuna Committee received 381 sets of answers from qualified medical men, 242 of wham testifSed to having seen 40 diseases either intensified or conveyed by vaccina- tion. So damning were the revelations, it appearss that the second part at the Committees transactions was suppressed! Anti-vaccinists confidently ask :. " fled these things been known generally when this vaccination legislation was being pushed through Parliament would any such measures ever have been allowed to become law / To this ques- tion there is but one answer possible. In this con- nection it may be well to note the answer of Mr. Fern to the present Royal Commission to the effect that despite his 20 years experienue as government examiner of vaccine lymph, he could not detect germs of diseases in it; nor could he guarantee the purity or safet3 of a single drop of that multiform substance A point is frequently made as to the absence or presence of smallpox in certain coun- tries and it is sought to base arguments thereon solely on vaccinal conditions. To that mode of generalising anti-vacciniste very sensibly demur. They decline to attach weight to any such partial and artificial conditions. They demand that all the factors of the problem be taken into account Otherwise the results must of necessity be mislead- ing and mischievous. Anti vaccmists point also to the significant fact that since the general adoption of vaccination in this country the fall in the rate of infant mortality has ceased, and they ' believe that the inflicting upon the infant population of a country of "an acute specific dis- ease," attended with "serious constitutional disturb- ance," is admirably calculated to, in various ways, indirectly increase the infantile death rate." To assert the contrary may be " scientific " but tol them it seems the reverse of common sense. Finally' they would point to a couple of recent instances of two experienced towns, Leicester practically non- vaccinated, and Darlington well vaccinated ; both towns showing admirable results from sanitary ' measures alone. An imaginative officialism, basing its results on random guesses, figures forth prepos- terous numbers of infants' lives saved annually by vaccination ! At Leicester from 1868-72 with over 90 per cent, of its births vaccinated, its death rate from all causes, of children under 5 years was 107 ; under ten, 61; and under fifteen, 45 per 1,000 living respectively. While in 1888-89 with only about 5 per cent, of primary vaccinations to births, each of these death-rates had fallen enormously. The death-rate under five years had declined to 63, that under ten years to 35 and that under fifteen years to 25 per 1,000 respectively. This is a result or at least a sequence, of Leicester's repudiation of vac- cination and resolute adherence to a sound policy of public hygiene. That well vaccinated town Darlington, shows in its way, equally striking results since it has reso- lutely embarked upon a policy of sanitary reform. There has been a very great diminution of zymotic disease generally, and a corresponding saving of life—vaccination going on all the same. The ages, unfortunately, are not given (as at Leicester, just quoted), in the letter of Mr. Alexander Wheeler, of Darlington, from which this statement as to Dar- _ _

, lington is quoted. Put it is typical and significant, and tends to confirm the anti-vaccinist contention, that safety from smallpox and other zymotic diseases is not to be found on Jennerian and Pas- teurian lines. With a state of things such as is above partly disclosed,it seems pretty well hopeless for the pro-vaccinist party,in and out of Parliament, much longer to keep the compulsory law on the statute look. The case of the anti-vaccinists, so far as the compulsory law is concerned, seems unas- sailable. J. 11.

div.head: WORCESTER ELECTION.
div.p: THE WORCESTER ELECTION.

Mr. Baron Pollock and Mr. Justice Wills gave judge- ment on Saturday in the election petition brou4ht against Mr. Allsopp, the sitting Conservative member. Mr. Baron Pollock said they had been trying not merely a case between the petitioner and respondent, but a , charge against toe city of Worcester. He would report to the Speaker of the House of Commons that there was no reason to believe that either corrupt and illegal prac- tices had extensively prevailed, or that they had been proved before them. It remained to consider whether any alleged corrupt practices,lmwever small in number, had been so brought home to the member or his agents as to void this election, which was a very difficult question. These were charges of a criminal character. and must be strictly proved. On the present occasion there was not only no strict proof, but the evidence fell far short of what was necessary to hold suei charges established. He had not only no doubt that the peti- tioner's case had not been proved, but he thought there ' had been a want of thought and consideration in the obringing forward a large nismber of charges that had never even been entered upon. He decided, therefore, that the petition insist be dismissed with costs. MT. Justice Wills concurred in this decision, saying that no seat would he safe if a member was liable to be unseated On such evidence. He at the same time remarked that the conduct of some Conservatives, such as Samuel Bowen and one or two others, if persisted in, would make them marked men whom an honourable candidate would be afraid to have anything to do with. He thought the grace of Christmas charities was lost when reference was made to them during an election.

div.head: PRESIDENT RARR/SON'S FAREWELL: MESSAGE.
div.p: PRESIDENT RARR/SON'S FAREWELL: MESSAGE.

President Harrison's farewell message was delivered to Congress on Tuesday. The retiring President asserts that the system of Protection has brought the country to a pitch of prosperity never before attained ; but he assumes that the recent election will be followed by tariff changes in favour of foreign producers. Ele re- commends the whole subject of tariff revision should be left for tht neat Congress to deal with. The foreign relations of the Republic are satisfactory, but General Harrison, writing in the spirit of his" Retaliation "pro- clamation against Canada, recommends that attempts should be made to deprive the Dominion of the trade which it now derives from the United States, and that the latter should obtain a separate waterway from the Great Lakes to the ocean. Referring to the Brussels Conference, General Harrison says it is too early yet to express an opinion as to the probable result. He recom- mends further legislation in order to meet Anglo- Canadian trade competition in: the Pacific, and advises Congress to support the American company which is engaged in the construction of the Nicaragua Canal. A revision of the quarantine regulations is recom- mended in order to prevent the invasion of plagues."

div.head: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN A GASWORKS.
div.p: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN A GAS- WORKS.
HORRIBLE NIMILITION OF WORKMEN.

A disastrous explosion of gas occurred on Saturday in the Valley-road Gasworks, the largest of the four gaswerks possessed by the Bradford Corporation. About noon a series of tar pits, situated in vaults, measuring about sixty yards by thirty, blew up with a great re- port. The whole surface of the ground was lifted into the air. Two great'condensers were destroyed, and the mains and houses were blown away. Twelve men were slacking coke from the retorts at the time, and of these five were severely injured, three being, it is stated, be- yond hope of recovery. One poor fellow fell into a pit of hot tar, and was rescued with difficulty. Another sustained a fractured skull. A horse and cart were burnt, but the man in attendance escaped unhurt. The driver of an engin, on the Midland Railway was blown off the locomotive. The destruction of property is I enormous. Nearly the whole building is rendered useless, but the gas for public lighting is being supplied from i other depots.

MEDICAL MALL, ABERDARE, WALES.
SHOOTING OUTRAGE BY A DISAPPOINTED LOVER.

On Monday, Charles Brace, blacksmith, of High Wyncli,Sawbridgeworth, was charged at Epping with shooting with intent to murder Mrs. Mary Winks. The prisoner attributed the breaking off of an engagement with Mrs. Winks's daughter to the mother, and on Saturday evening, as she was driving from Epping with her son, the prisoner shot her in the bead and body with a revolver. The son ran for assistance, and when ap- prehended the prisoner was found to have a revolver and 37 bullets in his possession. Mrs. Winks is in a most precarious state. The son having given evidence, the prisoner was remanded.

div.head: DIABOLICAL OUTRAGES ON A. RAILWAY. FOUR MEMPTS TO WRECK TRAINS.
div.p: DIABOLICAL OUTRAGES ON A. RAILWAY. FOUR MEMPTS TO WRECK TRAINS.

A Berwick correspondent states that another diaboli- cal attempt was made on Saturday morning to upset a train on the Berwick and Kelso branch of the North- Eastern Railway. As the train from Berwick was near- ing Ord, at about six o'clock, it ran into several sleepers which had been placed upon the metals, injuring the engine and delaying the train for about an hour. An arrest is expected. Former attempts had been ;lade within a few weeks to wreck trains on the North- Eastern, and how determined the last effort was is proved by the fact that the sleepers were fastened to the line by means of a thick wire. It is stated that the police believe that all four outrages have been per- formed by the sarne hand, and they hope shortly to have the culprit ia custody. The plonh of the swine was ;completely broken off.

div.head: SCOTCH BANK AGENT ATTACKED BY HIGHWAYMEN.
div.p: A SCOTCH BANK AGENT ATTACKED BY HIGHWAYMEN.

A Glasgow correspondent telegraphs :—On Saturday afternoon a robbery was committed on the highway be- tween Stomehouse and Larkhalt, Lanarkshire. Mr. Cunningham. the Larkhall agent of the Union Bank of Scotland, was returning home in a vehicle from Stone- house, where he calls every Saturday for the cash and papers of the branch bank at that place. While he was driving up a hilly part of the road two men sprang from the brushwood and attacked him and his clerk. Both robbers were ma.sked and carried revolvers. One of the men seized the horse, and the other, mounting the car- riage, presented a revolver at Mr. Cunningham and said " Give me the pAirl, or you will be dead in a moment." Mr. Cumairghatu resisted, and succeeded in removing the mask from one of the men. The other, however, made off with the bag containing cheques and vouchers. Mr. Cunningham returned to Stonehouse, and a large number of police from Hamilton were quickly on the track of the thieves. Two arrests were made during the evening. The affair has caused a great sensation in the locality.

div.head: WINDFALL FOR A FACTORY HAND.
div.p: WINDFALL FOR A FACTORY HAND.

A man named Bregan recently died in San Francisco leaving upwards of £.30,000, and bills were placarded in Lochee, Dundee, requesting, information regarding his relatives. The services of the police officials were en- listed in the matter, and they have, after making Inquiry, found that a man named John Thorns, living at Fite, and his sister, Elizabeth Thorns, a factory-worker, residing inilligh-street. Lochee, appear to be the heirs. It seems that their father was Brogan's nearest relative.

div.head: INHUMAN CONDUCT OF A. FATHER.
div.p: INHUMAN CONDUCT OF A. FATHER.
A WRETCHED FABITLY.

The Bolton magistrates on Saturday investigated a shocking case of cruelty to children by John Williams, labourer, which occurred in August, 1891, he having then left his wife and family. One morning a child, three years old, was found with its face saturated with blood. It was covered with bruises from top to bottom. The nose was cut and chafed, and the right side swollen all the injuries being inflicted by Williams. Be was committed to prison for three months.

The Cry TUE national conference .on the .Fc causes of and remedies for agricultu"

Protection. rat depression, which was opened in London on ThursdaV,will, hereafter,we are afraid, be spoken of as a great opportunity lost. The idea of this conference originated amongst Lancashire farmers, but they seem to have had very little to do with the Organisation of it. The work of mani- pulation, the drawing up of the resolutions, and the general ordering of the conference fell into other hands, and as a result, instead of a great gathering composed exclusively, or almost ex- clusively, of tenant farmerh, we have a so-called national" conference, preiided over by Mr. Jas. LOWTHER, and with a platform upon which one landlord crowded upon the heels of another. There were, for example, Mr. HENRY CHAPLIN, M.P., re- lieved from the restraints of office ; the Earl of WINCHILSEA, the Marquis of HUNTLEY, Mr. P. A. MoNTz, M.P., and numerous others. It is not to the interest of landlords that there should be * full and frank discussion of agricultural depres- sion bY those who feel most directly where the shoe pinches. In Stich a dis- cussion there would Of necessity he a great deal said that would have a tendency to weaken that inequitable land system from which spring a great many of the hardships that the occupying culti- vators of English land have to endure. It is not surprising, therefore, thst,at the very opening of the Conference care was taken to "draw a red herring across the scent," as one of the disap- pointed delegates described the process. The "red herring ' was a rcsolution demanding, amongst other thing*, protection for agriculture, in other words, a tax upon the bread stuff's of the people. This resolution was, after a discussion u which those who wore opposed to it were hureLY

div.p: :-.aocarded a hearing, carried by a vote of about three to one. . It is noteworthy that the most eativnuous opponents of the resolution were the • representatives of northern farmers. Mr. BAR- Low, a 'delegate from Lancashire, said the firmers •whom he represented, although they • were • the- means of' getting the 'Conference • called • •together, had been so dissatisfied with the selection of subjects for discussion that they had almost decided to withdraw from the Con ference. It they had been 'permitted, he added, to frame the programme, they would have given the most important places to the questions of rent and land tenures, both of which subjects had been left in. the background. lie, concluded his address by the.emphatic assertion that what was • wanted was a 'better system of land tenure, with security for the tenants' improvements. Mr. I! DUTTON, of the Chester Farmers' Club, was equally . strong in his protests against embarking on a hopeless , crusade for Protection, and he men- tioned ,at. the club he represented had declared against it by two to one. Other northern dele- gates also-lvarned the Conference of the futility • of any,,attempts:to tax the bread of the people, for the purpose of bolstering up *rents and staving . off radical reforms of the land kiwis. But all this was at no avid'. '• The Conference had been very completely- q nobbled" by Tory politicians and Ptoter;tionist, intriguers. The result is that, so far af; this Conference is concerned, the cause of 1 the " depressed " farmer has received very little advancement.' ,'The hopelessness of any remedy which involves the taxing of the food, of the • masses of the people, is too obvious to need en- '.larging upon, especially when there' are other' more adequate methods of dealing with the' diffi- . faulty.

• ROCHESTER is famous just now for an election petition, but it deserves recognition for another • reason. IL contains a clergyman who is not afraid of tackling one of the abstrusest of problems. '4This clergyman tells us that it has been stated by aevery competent authority, whose state,ment has not been contradicted, that forty years ago when wheat was sixty shillings the• quarter, bread was , the same price as at present, when wheat is sold ,at twenty-seven- shillings the quarter. He. has, - therefore, come'to the conclusion that a consider- able amount of rrofit must be absorbed by the middlemen who intervene between the farmer and the consumer. In this opinion he is confirmed by the local variations in the price of bread. In Rochester, the quartern loaf is fivepence ; in Gravesend, fivepence half-penny, and in Lincoln- shire fourpence, a difference of twenty-five per eent. It was only a few days ago that a corres- pondent of a London newspaper, set out to solve the problem which as exercised the mind of the Rochester clergyman, but after a good deal of perambulation and much inquiry in both the " West End " and the "East End," the only . definite conclusion lie could arrive at, was that • there were more mysteries in the bakor's business • than he had dreamed of.

Mr. HOPWOOD, the Recorder of Liverpool, must, . one might imagine, feel considerably flattered by the attention. which is paid .him by Mr. JUSTICE i GRANTHAM. MT. Horwook) has won a great reputatiOn by the bold and unswerving manner in which he has advocated—and practised in his own court—a more lenient treatment in the matter of imprisonment of persons convicted of criminaloffenees. Justice GRANTHAM seems to be . ambitious to achieve g reputation as the special critic of Mr. Hommel:es method. It is not many weeks since he went rather, out of his way in a northern town -to speak disparagingly of the Liverpool Recorder's • ideas, sad en Tuesday in addressing the Grand Jury at the opening of Liverpool Assizes he returned to the congenial theme. He had been amused, he said, when on coming into this county he read t wci addresses delivered by two learned gentlemen—die Recorder of Liverpool and the Recorder of Manchester. The onalaimed that the diminution of crime was du*tO'his method of giving short sentences while the .other asserted it was the result of the 'long sentences he was *in the habit of giving. This is no doubt contradictory so far as the two Re- a Orders are-concerned, but, rightly regarded, and :.aseuming that there had been something like an equal diminution of crime in Liverpool and Man- chester, it is a complete justification of the policy .of Mr. HOPWOOD. Punishment by imprisonment is not for the nurpse of brutalising the prisoner but fer the prevention of crime, and if it be found from experience that crime is no more prevalent where short sentences are given than where .long sentences find favour, there is very little to be said in defence of the latter. A long term ofrthe degrading. servitude of a prison is much more likely to manufacture and turn out upon society.a hardened and impenitent criminal than is a short term.

HOW TO SELL CHEAPLY.

Mr. R. Kilpatrick, the inspector of weights and measures for Widnes division, had recently received complaints from stall holders in Widnes market, that a hawker from Addlington-street, Liverpool, named Margaret Brown, was underselling them, although she had to pay the same price as themselves for their goods. He consequently paid her a visit on Saturday last and found on her stall two one lb. weights, gas of which was ui drachms light and .the other two drachms light. , This was the reason the woman could sell so cheaply, remarked the Inspector to the Widnes Magistrates on 'Thursday,and she was ordered to pay 10s. and ccsts, her weights to be forfeited—Edward Lawrence Bent, of Springfield-street, Liverpool, also a stall holder in Widnes market, was mutetttcl in .m similar penalty for being in possession of a 21b. weight which was 15* drachms JoSEpIZ PRITC MOLD has the heat stock of ladies silver and gold watches In the town.—Advt.. AN EXASPERATED WOMAN AT RUNCORN.

Ann Waller, wife of a Bhip Canal employA, living in Ashridge-st., was summoned before theltuncorn mag- istrates, on MondAy, to answers charge of having wil- fully damaged the goods of Elizabeth Barnes, of 2, Duke-st. Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant, and Mr.' Humphreys for the defence. It appeared that on Saturday night, the 26th ult., at a quarter to eleven, the defendant went to Mrs. Barnes's house, made use of foul namos to her, and, on being pushed through the doorway, smashed five panes of glass in the window, and the splinters of glass were scattered amongst; the confectionery, and boxes of sweets, boiled ham. Sic., do- ing damage to the extent of £l.—Mr. Humphreys said the defendant was suffering under a sense of the most grievous wrong a woman could receive at the hands of her husband, and in a fit of exasperation she broke the windows.—The defendant was fined el and costs 14s. 6d., and was also ordered to pay 10s. damage. A sum- mons for assault was not heard because of an informal- ity. In default of paying the money, the defendant was sent to gaol for 14 days.

The dead iT10537,:i;-m—an. -&;;iiti --it-ire-a- Collier, 34 years of age, a postman who had resided at 17, Thomas- st., Widnes, was found floating in a silver refining tank at the Thursis Copper Works on Snnday evening. About twelve months ago Collier had a severe attack of influenza, which left him bereft of memory and speech, and with a mind deranged. The portal authorities allowed him a pension of 13s. a week. On Saturday he visited the house of his sister in Peelhouse-lane,whence he departed about 3.30 in the afternoon, refusing the ser- vices of the kid who usually accompanied him home. Re did not turn up at home, and search was made for him without avail. On Sunday afternoon, about three o'clock, a girl named Fleys saw him in Major Cross-st., with his clothing wet through, and she advised him to go home, but he only stared blankly at her. Two hours later he was found a 3 described. Ele had to ascend some steps to reach the tank, which contained 2ft. 7in, of liquid. Mr. F. A. Jones, ;be deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body on Tuesday afternoon, and a ver- dict to the effect that he committeed suicide while tem- porarily insane was returned. The deceased leaves a widow and three children. ,

NEARLY every Englishman is under the impres- sion that he can stand, or walk, or run, and indeed disport himself pretty much as he likes on a country highway, so long as he does not obstruct the passage or interfere with the equal liberty of anyone else. But notions of that sort should be dispelled by a judgment which was given in the Court of Appeal on Saturday. From that judgmentit would appear that a man must not presume so far upon his supposed right to the use of a highway as to interfere with the pleasures of a ducal shooting party. Briefly put, the cir- cumstances which led up to the judgment of the Court of Appeal were these. In October, 1891,the Du la§ of RumaND,accompanied by a "dis- tinguished "party were shooting on some moors in Derbyshire, when a man named HARRISON, a saw-handle maker, living near Sheffield, came along a public footpath close by. HARRISON did not move away so expeditiously as the ducal party wished him to do, and, it was alleged, he wilfully interfered with the shooting by loitering on the road. He was warned by LORD EDWARD MANNERS to move on, but as he did not choose to do that, he was seized by three keepers, thrown down upon the road, and held there for three-quarters of an hour. In consequence of this .he brought an action for damages against the DAME of Enna/fp and other members of the 'shooting party, but after a two days' hearing a jury decided 'that the five shillings which had been paid ,into court was. sufficient to satisfy the plaintiffs decision was appealed against, the DUKE of Rumex», in his turn, applied for an injunction to restrain the plaintiff from interfering with his shooting pleasures. In its result this reference to the Court of Appeal was a victory,for the DUKE of RUTLAND secured a victory all along the line. The appeal of the saw-handle maker was dismissed, and the injunction to restrain him from coming between the nobiliiiand their game was granted. There is something ahout this case,,that should be highly gratifying to admirers ot,the "good old times." It shows that an aristocrat can still, under certain Arcumstances, 4Check in a rough and peremPtory way the presumption' of the poor plebeiin who dares to come between him and his sport. On the other hand, the case will remind those who prefer modern liberty and equality to ancient privilege that the old feudal bias has not yet by any means been altogether climina'tesl from English car

RUNCORN Vk:ESLEYAN CIRCUIT TEMPERANCE SOCIETT.

The annual meeting was held on Thursday evening in Halton-road chapel, under the presidency of Mr. Tim- perley. There was a good attendance. The Chairman having delivered an address, Mr. J. D. Jones, the secre- tary, read the report of the Temperance Committee of the Conference of 1892, which showed there were 3,882 bands ot hope with amembershipof 400,167 ; an increae of 168 bands andof 28,627 members. The number of teoek-r..rice S. etieties is 836, an increase of 64, with 52,058 members, an ir.crease ef 513.—1 n the course of an address the Rev. Jas. Hanby referred to the bishop of Chester's liconsiog propos ds„ and said he was ready to give then, a trial if they could not get anything better. Once get, the power shifted from the magistrates into the hands of representative bodies, and the will of the people should decide. To educate the poople was the duty of the Church, and he hailed the speedy approach of Sunday Chzing, and Local Option in some shape or form. Bis appeal to every Iceor of his fellow man was by persenal example and unremitting zeal, to promote the cause of sobriety, and the .removal of drunkenness from the world. (ApplAuse.) The Rev. . arrowstnith also spike, and described the evils occasioned by the drink traffic. As to remedial measures ha suggested that as a first step temperance reformers ought to bend their energies to securing the closing of public-houses on the liird's day. Sunday drinking was a national curse. Sunday closing had practically the unanimous support of Churches. Not long ago the Wesleyan Methodist Church presented a petition containiug 596,877 signatures. In many instances publicans were not averse to it. The present Government and its supporters were to a large extent pledged to Sunday Closing. Promised support of moral reforms had much to do with giving them power, and if they betrayed their trust the democracy would smite them hip and thigh. The number of licensed houses ought to be reduced. Be spoke thankfully that last year 230 renewals were refused, and declared that the whole question of issuing and withholding licenses would only be satisfactorily settled when it was referred to the will of the people. Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: RIJRCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RIJRCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting .was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. Mr. Jas. Pritchard presided,and there were present, the Rey. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi,Dr. McDougall,Messrs. A. tialkeld, T. Hunley,S. Taylor, and G. Moss (clerk).

SCHOOL ATTHNDANCE.PRIVATH ADVHNTCHH SCHOOLS. Tee School Attendance Committee reported that 107 parents had been summoned to attend before them, and 91. appeareil. Prialeei,l6 were ordered to be taken egaiuet 1 parents. The visitors' returns for the month were read, and ,sll.)wed a percentage of atteridancS of 82, is compared with 82.4 in the corresponding period of last year, the slight falling off in regularity being mainly in the Infants' schools. ~The average attendance was 3,069, against 2,971 last year. There was an in- crease of 141 children on the rolls. In answer to Dr. McDougall, Dr. Gastaldi said the parents that had ap- peared before the Committee were the same " old fainily " that had troubled them eo long.—Mr. Handley remarked that the Committee had also had the usual difficulty, with the boat people who had no homes lon shore. There were no means of getting the children of these people to school.—Dr. Gastauli said during the past year they had great d'fficulty with regard to the so-cailed private schools. The majority of these peo- ple brought before the Com mit tre tried to evade the Board by the tactics of sending their children to such institutions. They found through the agency of their officers that many did not attend them who were stated to be doing so. It was merely a subterfuge to evade the Board, and he thought it was a degrading fast. Many parents had done„everything in their power to get their children to absent themselves from sehool month after month. He asked what power the' Board had with reference to these private schools.—Canon Wood said if the children were not properly educated the Board could say that they were " not efficiently edu- cated," and thus deal with them. He inquired if these schools kept any register.—The Clerk .replied in the negative, and even if they did they would not show them to the Board's officers.—Ttie Chairman : Is there any increase in private adventure schonls ?—The Clerk replied that there had been an increase of one, but since the subject was last before the Committee it had been closed. That school was a harbour for bad attenders. It was difficult to deal with children attending such institutimis, and it was only possible to do SO on the ground, that they were inefficiently taught. The magistrates eould examine them.—Mr. Handley : lam afraid you would not get the magistrates to go to that trouble.—The Chairman expressed the hope that before long the Legisla- Cure would give them power to deal with sueli natters.— Mr. 'Vylor said se far as he understood, they had no reason to believe that children were not efficiently faught in these private adventure echoole.—Dr. Gas- taldi said he had examined some children who could not ! make a figure or write their own names.—Dr. • McDougall said it appeared that the fines iiiflicted by : the magistrates had no effect, a..d he urged that the Board should ascertain wheper those in charge of these schools were efficient and qualified to teach. He sug- gested that the Clerk should,,go can fully through the Education Act of 070, to sae what powers the Board possessed in the matter. He thought, as a matter of fact, it would be e ise to confer with other Boards on the subject and endeavour to act in concert in drawing up a memorial to the Education Department. He pro- posed a resolution to the effect.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

The Chairman said the last School Board petitioned the Education Department to alter the date of the triennial election, foam the end of Docembor to a more ccnvenient date, and they complied with the request. As a result, the last election was held en the 10th December. In regard to the forthcoming election, returning officers only received the order on Friday lest, which compelled him to fix the election for the 30th inst. This was very inconvenient.—During the dis- cussion that ensued, it appeared that the Education Department, if any one, were at fault, and not the returning officer, who did not bold the position when the alteration was made. It was generally considered that it was a subject to be dealt with by the new Board.

div.head: COTTON CRISIS.
div.p: THE COTTON CRISIS.
NEW MOVE BY THE EMPLOYERS.

A new movement was made on Thursday, by the masters, who have convened a conference for Friday next, with a view to endeavouring to induce the employ- ers of south and north-east Lancashire, tl assist those of the northeast, by adopting short time. A previous effort about a fortnight ago in the same direction failed, but it is considered vital to the interests of the employers , that the hands who are in work should he prevented from helping those who are now out, and strenuous efforts will be made at the conference to prevail upon the employers of the northern portion of the county to make some sacrifice. Considerable distress already pre- vails among the non-unionists out of employment, and a suggestion of a relief fund bas been made. .

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Although the University extension Lectures so far as Runcorn is cisncerned have come to an end, it is pleasing to find that the Free Library Combait- tee have stepped into the vacant place, and have arranged a series of lectures of a somewhat similar character. The lecturers announced are local gen- tlemen well qualified to deal with the subjects chosen. *Web will be found of interest and instruc- tion. The first lecture is announced for Wednes- day evening next, when Mr. Thomas Ward,the well known director of the Salt Union, will describe the action of water in the formation of the earth's crust.

The analysis of the water supply of the Water- works Company, included in the report of Dr. McDougall, also requires thorough investigation. Dr. Bell states that the water is such that he could not recommend it for a town like Runcorn, but that gentleman is alleged to have described the water as being good to the County Council, and, as Mr. Smith pertinently pointed out,the two statements are alto- gether inconsistent. The figures given by Dr. Bell. show the water to be exceptionally " hard," which, it appears, Mr. Wiswall has ascertained can be re- medied to some extant by pumping about half the quantity of water that is at present drawn from the bowels of Runcorn Hill. No doubt before the pur- chase of the undertaking is effected by the Commis- sioners this and other questions will be probed to the bottom, and the best course for the ratepayers to pursue will be to suspend their judgment until they are in possession of the complete facts.

Since the formation of the United Alkali Cam- party and the consequent exodus from Widnes of the manufacturers who were members of the Widnes Bench of magistrates, there has been a constant lack of those qualified to dispense justice in the local police court. It is an almost, daily occurrence for the police to search for a magistrate to clear the'eeflet'of—tf•eir ocCn panl a, and delays at the weekly sitting of the Petty Sessions have also be- come very frequent. On Thursday the business was delayed for an hour, through only one magis- trate mairing an appearance, and at the end of that time the services of Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, who happily chanced to be at home, were secured, and .the summonses and charges dealt with. Two pro- fessional men and all concerned these constant delays area serious matter. It would be well if the Town Council at, once considered the advisabil- ity of forming a borough bench, so that a number of gentletnen can he put upon the Commission of , the peace, who reside in the town, and who will therefore be more easily available and can conduct I thet,business in turn, without inconvenience to themselves or loss of time to-those who are under the union unate necessity to use the Police Court.

The Mayoral vkit to S. Nut's Church, op. Sunday last was an interesting and unique sight to the people of Widnes. /be presence of the volunteers, tire brigade, and police in the pro- cession, imparted a more imposing character to the function, hut the slor!. distance they ha to tra- verse, • nearly across the Town Hall Sqttare, not give scope fir an adeqitate display. The action or tne Catholic members of the Council, in leiving i-lie ,ranks at the entrance to the church,and thenc, pro- ceeding to their own play«, of worship, gave rias to much cornmeal, but cl.aritit de criticism would make allowance for the fact dist they were simply acting up to the scruples of their faith. And can more be asked of religious men? One cholla help thinking, however, that their' might have carried their courtesy to the Mayor a -oil' further, and en- tered the sacred edifice, or, irth-iir r•ligious scrupu- losity knows no concession, that it would have been better to have refrained from attending the function than have made str-h an exhibition. There was nothing in the sermoir of the vicar to which the adherent. of any sect might not have listened with interest and lit...fit, and if the Corporation act in their transactions uuon the high lines of duty, sketched by thelpreacher, th- r ttepayera will have no rsason to regret the fir,r Mayoral visit to church.

The able report of Dr. McDougall. medical 'officer of health to hnincorn Board of Commis- tnissioners, which is reproduced in these columns in'ri curtailed form," dealing with the epidemic of typhoid fever, which prevailed during the summer and autumn, discloses a condition of things that cannot be viewed with equanimity by the rate- payers. The doctor points out that in a number of the cases reported upon, it is difficult to account fel the presence of fever, beyond . what applies to almost the whole of the town, namely, the faulty principl., on which ashpits and privie are con- structe.rl In consequence of this bad cone, ruction, Dr. McDougall has seen sewage matter penetrating under the houses, and in his last annual report he suggested to the Beard that. if they were not pre- pared to require the adoption of water carriage generally, they should at all events insist on the more modern system of privy and ashpit construc- tion. This suggestiani would seem. to have been al- together disregarded. atm', he present exposure by the medical officer practically amounts to an im- peachment of the Board of Commissioners. They cannot plead ignorance of the defects in the sani- tary arrangements of the town, or of the evil tektite that must follow the wholesale poisoning of the atmosphere by these seething tanks of rotten- ness, called ashpits. lii fact they have known for years of the defects in their byelaw, but have hesitated to improve them even in.a slight degree, from fear that the Local Government Braind would inaist on more radical changes, by the adoption of their model byelaws. The Board of Commissioners can only relieve themselves of any responsibility for future outbreaks, by. prompt and decisive actir.n. At present:the report is referred to the consideration of the Health Committee, and the position they take upon the question, will be eagerly awaited. . ,
TtEE TYPHOID FEVER EPIDEMIC AT
RUNCORN. DEFECTIVE BUILDING BYELAW&

At the last meeting of Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, Dr. McDougall, the medical officer of health, presented a report on the prevalence of en- teric fever within the Authority's Sanitary District for the ten months ending the 31st of October last. Seventy-two notifications were recei red; seven of these were duplicates, reducing the number of in- fected cases to sixty-five. These were distributed over thirty-eight streets. In addition tethese noti- fied as typhoid fever, sixty-six were reported as continued fever. Several of these cases occurred in small back-to-back houses, which are receiving the attention of the Authority. Thee.., cases were notified chiefly from the localities in which typhoid fever prevailed. Fifteen detail* In-en ete-erie, fever were registered during these ten a,nth'. "rile niost notice". able feature of interest WWI the notification of fourteen Cases Practically from one block of property. Hem.. tunately, owing to the public works now in progreei in the neighbourhood. these houses were, like many others in some parts of the town, very Much overcrowded, and I regret to say that in some instances the houses were not kept as clean as they might be. This I may say is always the case wherever there is overcrowding. The drainage arrangements for these houses coutd not be held to be responsible for the outbreak ef fever, for there are no drains nearer than the opposite side of the street, with a large space beyond. In order to clear up as far far as possible the outbreak, a sample of the water supply was sent to the county analyst. His report, although not describing the water as of high quality, did not indicate that sewage matter had actually found its way into it. In order to have no doubt in this mat- ter, a second sample was sent to Somerset House for atialytisoind the Somerset House authorities practically confirmed the results of the county analyst. The analysis of the water only yielded negative results, and it was necessary to carry the investigation further. At- tention was then directed towards

THE MILE SUPPLY OF TRH NEIGHBOURHOOD, and it was found that this was obtained practically from one cart. The water supply on the farm which supplied the milk was taken from a well about 75 feet deep, with two pigstyes about 14 feet distant, and a cesspool on the other side about 30 feet distant, also a manure heap about 70 feet away. A sample of this water was sent to the county analyst. Although the analyst does not point to any distinct sewage contamina- tion, it is difficult to avoid coming to the conclusion that sewage matter must have found its way into the well, owing to the proximity of the pigstyes and cesspool before mentioned, It is only fair to state that no case of fever had occurred on the farm, but as a matter of pre- caution the consumers of this milk in the infected neigh- bourhood were advised to boil it before use. The recru- descence of enteric fever for the last three years has in the present year deserted its former haunts, snd invaded the north-east part of the town. In a number of these cases it is difficult to account for the presence of fever, beyond what applies to almost the whole of the town, viz., the faulty principle on which ashpits and privies are constructed. The method hitherto in use wss to dig a hole in the furthest off paA of the yard for a privy and ashpit. These holes were at one time of considerable dimensions, and in many instances were largo enough to hold cartloads of the seething mass of fermenting oecue

Ilent matter. But, unfortunately, the evil does not all end there. The subsoil of the yards gets thoroughly soaked with sewage matter, and in some ins:ances I have seen it penetrating under the houses, owing to the faulty principle on which all these conveni- ences have been made. I may here mention that this condition of things is considerably aggravated in those localities where the houses are built over a substratum of clay. I had occasion recently to in- spect the lavatory arrangements of one of the largest schools in the town, and found what might be termed without any exaggeration a monster open astmit. It measures 43ft. in length, is 3ft. 6in. wide, and is of considerable depth. At the date of my visit it contain- ed a large quantity of liquid sewage, making it difficult to get at its exact depth. I am informed by the nuisance inspector that it takes days to empty this huge sewage trough, and you can well imagine the unwholesome character of the surrounding atmosphere. It has a range of 13 privies, which provide accommodation for over 1,000 children. Apart from the risk of fever occurring in these localities, it is obvious that these insanitary conditions must be held to be highly detrimental to health. This state of things has grown up owing to the defective building bylaws. Had these building bylaws been re-modelled and reconstructed, those difficulties which I have mentioned would have been obviated in the case of the more recently constructed dwellings. In my last annual report I suggested to the authority that if they were not prepared to require the adoption of water carriage generally, they should at all events insist on the more modern system of privy and ashpit construction. Several cases of enteric fever were removed to the isolation hospital, and disinfectants were used freely in the infected localities. In visiting some of the infected parts of the town I found that fever had occurred in single or b tck to back houses. It is impostible in these houses to get thorough ventilation, and I would advise the authority to require the owner to eonvert these into double houses.

First, I would advise that the nuisance inspector be relieved of other duties except those which appertain to his office. Second, that the nuisance inspector be re- quired to make a house to house visitation, giv- ing a. detailed account of the condition of yards, pas- sages entries, ashpits, and privies in a systematic man- ner, and that his report of work done be placed before the Health Committee at their fortnightly meetings. Thirdly, that one uniform method be a lop ed to make ashpits and privy pits watertight, and that as far as practicable one uniform size be adopted, and that of small dimenilions. Fourth, that in all courts and crowded localities water carriage be insisted on. Filth, that all yards be properly laid in ene uniform manner, say with smooth brick, or some other suitable material, properly laid with a fall from all parts of the yard to the grid, which should he kept as far away from the back door and windows as possible. Sixth, all entries and back passages should be laid, say with smooth brick, and made to fall towards a grid, so as to make it iinpos- sible for the subsoil to become saturated with sewage. Seventh, all old brick and stone drains should be taken out, and replaced by socket pipes of suitable sizes. Eighth, milkhouses and cowsheds, should be systemati- cally visited, and periodical reports presented to the Health Committee as to the source of milk supply and infringements cf rnilkhouse regulations. Ninth, all hones registered as lodgings under the Sanitary Act of 1866 should be frequently visited and reported upon as to overcrowding, ventilation, and general cleanliness. Common indzing-houses are regulated by special lit h ,vs, and are required to be reported on periodically. Tenth, all house drains should be syphoned before joining the main sewers, one in every ease vetitilated in the house side of the evphon trap. Hitherto there were six sewer nutlets, ssliereas now there is but nee Elereath, all new houses intended to he used as d'a- shuutl,hef•re occupation,be inepected and reported upon by the surveyor, and the record preserved for reference. In hit report on the atialyia of the town's water, Dr. Carter Bell, the county analys-, points nut thet the euliel matter is very high and consists chiefly of chlnrides. As regarded the Organic matter it wee a 4. but 1 mild not recommend this water for the -itiprdy of a town like Runcorn." In a later, ismiinunication Dr. Bell s4ys the total solid matter at 212 degree 3 F is 84'58 grains per galloa ; mineral 52-92 grains per gallon ; loss in ignition 31.64 -rains per gallon; chlorire 11.90 I•il'AiTLI per gallon ; free ammonia in million parts -005, kluniin- ized ammonia in million parte .13. The analyst of Seinerset House statal The water is remarkably free from oronic impurity, and it?, suitability far dietetic purraases depends en-irely Upon the view whiati may he taken of the effect of the alkaline chlorides present, and this, in my opinion, is a question for.votir medical officer of health." The report has been referred to the Health Committee for their consideration and report.
WIDNES CORPORATION AT CHURCH.

One of the most honoured observances of a• muni- cipal corporation is the attendance once a year at some place of divine worship, and the Mayor of Widnes, Mr. F. 11. Gossage, took the earliest oppor- tunity of initiating the custom in Widnes. At the first meeting of the complete Qouncil, the Mayor invited the aldermen and councillors to accompany him to St. Paul's Church, and on Sunday morning when 'the'fiiimtioti took place, there was only one member of the Council absent. The procession from the Town Hall to the church, a very short distance, Was witnessed by a large crowd of ratepayers, to most of whom such an affair was a novelty. Leading the aay were 35 members of the police force, under Superinten- dent Keighley and Inspector Pattinson followed by Mr. Whittle, the attendant at the Town Irian, who was at- tired in his official uniform and carried a wand upon his shoulder. Then came the Mayor, whose form was hidden beneath an imposing robe, and whose head was crowned by the Mayoral hat; and on either skits of his worship walked Mr. J S. Gilliat, M.P., and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P. Immediately behind walked the Town Clerk (Mr. H. S. Oppenheim) wearing his wig and eown, and suc- ceeding' Caine Aldermen J. W. Wareing, H. S. Timmis, J. Williamson, J. Tilley, and S. Sadler; Councillors T. Shuttlewsirth, P. Langton, C. E. Barlow, T. A. Bullough, W. Christie, F. Neil, 0. Neil, S. Owens, Cr. Davies. Quinn, H. Singleton, J. Fitzpatrick, H. B. Shores, T, Carney. J. Gough. T. Smith, and W. Hodgkinson. Fol- lowing were Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst, S. Robinson, J. H. Lee, and W. Sadler, members of the Free Library Com- mittee: The officials who also joined in the procession were Messrs. T. Craik (assistant town clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), J. Woodend (clerk), J. S. Sinclair (sur- veyor), I. Carr (engineer), De. O'Keeffe (medical officer), W. Lowe 'sanitary inspector). C. Whitfield (collector), J. Shepherd (market inepector), C. H. Lewin (deputy magis- trates'clerk), and .H. Ds nby (clerk to the School Board). The members of the fire hriessie were in charge of Fore- man Barrow,and the rear was brmight up by a portion of the volunteer corps, commanded by Captain Lewis. On arriving at the church gates the police lined each side of the pathway leading, to the entrance of the church, and the precession passed between their ranks. At the church door the Catholic members of the Council with- drew and proceeded to their respective places of worship. The sacred edifice was crowded, but special seats had been reserved for the Corporation. The prayers were read by the Rev. R. Meiklejohn, and the lesehns by the Rees G. ft. Garrett, vicar, who also preached a sermon from the words " Whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God," Corinthians x. 31. The preacher said it. was with sincere pleasure that he welcomect the members of the Corporation within these walle that day. The text brought them back to the fundamental facts of their faith. They believed man WAS created by Almighty God, redeemed by Him, and should live for Him. In this living for the glen. of God there was surely an aim, an object, and an idea, which might well inspire every home, which Might well absorb the talents of every man. There was in those words a line of duty and :Ictien ni very special importance to those present, who had undertaken an important charge, and were now putrosted cith very vs:liable property. It was a serotra essponsis bility, for it was to the Corporation that the people looked for protection as far as human skill could go from the daneers of diseases, and it was on them the duty devolved of caring for the sick, especially among the poorer CIASS, no that their suffering might be alleviated. It was their duty to see by what means-they could lessen the temptations which beset everyone, so that righteousness would be made easier, and trans- gression and sin more difficult. • In all these tasks they would desire the aid of Almighty God. They might con- sider that these were only trifles, but it was attention to trifles that produced perfection, which was no trifle. The same remarks applied to the officials, upon whom depended to a great extent the smooth working, and the success of the Corporation. One duty he had mentioned was the care of the sick. He was thankful that at the very outset the Council had determined to increase the hospital accommodation, and he pleaded with them that morning to assist the funds connected with the hospitals which were suppirted by the rates, and in his opinion rightly so too. But there were occasions when nume- rous thiugs were required for the comfort and isenefit of the patients, which could not very well be chargeable upon the rates. In conclusion the rev. gentleman urged upon the congregation to endeavour by divine help to do all things unto the glory of God. The service con eluded by singing the first verse of the National Anthem, after which the procession returned to the rown Hall. The collection realised £22.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

--- The triennial election of Runcorn School Board, has been fixed by the returning officer, Mr. John Aehton,for Friday the SOth inst. Nominations have to be made on or before the nineteenth, the list of candidates will be published on the 21st, and with- drawals will he accepted up to four p.m., on the 23rd inst. In this month's issue of the Parish Magazine the Vicar thus alludes to the coming contest : THE VICAR'S VIEWS. Alas lit seems not unlikely that a School Board elec- tion may come and disturb us all at that season of the year when we should like to be of one heart and one mind. But if some of our citizens are not content with the quiet Board which has devoted itself to looking after its schools and making them thoroughly efficient, we cannot help it. Church people, and indeed all who

I think that Board schools and Church schools, and Wes- ' leyan schools and Roman Catholic schools should work = in peace and harmony for the common good of Runcorn will be obliged to resist any attempt to push the educa- tional theories of any restless spirits into practical competition with the old schools of he town. Compe- tition is an admirable thing in its way. If a group of advanced thinkers wish to compete with our Denominational schools let them put their hands into. their 0 CV,II pockets. But you and I have an objection to • their rating us compulsorily,putting their hands into our - pockets, and using our money to make it difficult te carry on our schools. If we have a contest, I fear I shall have many -more things to trouble you with." It is true that the election comes at an inconvenient and, therefore, inappropriate time, but it is difficult to find a cause for the wailing " also " of the rev. Canon. The legislature in its wisdom has decreed that an eleo- tion shall take place every third year, and the duty of constituting a new board devolves upon the ratepayers, and not upon any one,or even the whole,of the members who are called upon to vacate their seats. The sweet. complacency in which the Vicar sits in judgment upon himself and his colleagues, and pronounces the verdict or a "quiet 'and " oevoted " board, and the gentle re- signation conveyed in the words " we cannot help it, if the citizens are not content, form a picture one would not readily miss. In his own person be combines the function of judge, jury, counsel,and prisoner at the bar, -and who can wonder that the sentence is not the imposition of a penance, but a blessing. But it is not impossible that the ratepayers. however unpleasant it may be for the Vicar to be brought to the bar of public opinion, will insist on exer- cising the franchise and choosing their own representa- tives and not those upon whom he is pleased to t estow his benediction. It is surprising that the Vicar should have had the hardihood to pen the sentence " But you and I have an objection to their rating us cofhpulsorily, putting their hands into our pockets, and using our money to make it difficult to carry on our schools." What are the facts P The Vicar receives from the taxes of the country for his school a larger sum than the whole of the School Board rate for Runcorn. The total in- come of the Parish Church schools for the year ended June last was £1,384 ss. 7d., towards which the Vicar and his supporters contributed the trifling sum, in comparison, of £76 14s. Government supplied no less than £1,021 12s. 81, and tbe parents of children attending the school were taxed in the shape of school pence to the extent of £238 18s. Daring the last month there were 31 more children in average attendance at Greenway-road schools' than there was acoomosodation for, and in that month the average is always very low. In September, when children were better able to attend school there was , overcrowding to the extent o: 49 places, or in other words there were 530 children crowded in a building certified to accommodate only 481. But the denomina- tionalists led by the Vicar, would as soon think of pro- posing to extend the free education in the town, by an addition to the Board School, as he would of yielding obedience to the Pope. Is it therefore, to the interests of the ratepayers to return men to manage their schools whose chief desire is to check their growth ? There should only he one answer to that question in the poll- ing booths three weeks hence. The practical competition of which the denomination- alists are afraid is Free Education. With all their love for the education of youth, in secular and religious sub- jects, they never think it necessary to inform the parents that they can have it free for the asking. No. They wish to continue to receive the nation's taxes, and the children's pence in order to teach the doctrines contained within the four corners of their own religious creed, which, however good for the soul are not offered without price on a week day. It should be clearly understood that every person in England who sends his child to an elm mentary school has a right to free education. If the managers of a voluntary school refuse free admission, a complaint to the Education Department will secure it for them, Irrespective of any inquiry into the parents' means, and if the ratepayers of Runcorn desire to procure this great boon they will send to the School Board men who will support and aid them in their efforts to cOtain it, and whose cbject is to give to the rising generation a thoroughly efficient edncation, irrespective of party or creed.
AN INTERPERA.rE-40TIfER AND HER. CHILDREN.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday. before Messrs. C. Reynolds and J. Handley, & middle-sized woman named Margaret Hardly, who appeared in the dock very poorly clad, was brought up under a warrant issued at the instance of tne Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to • Children, charging her with wilfully neglecting and exposing her three children aged twelve, nine, and seven, thereby causing them unnecessary suffering likely to injure their health. Mr. J. S. Ford, the society's in- spector from Chester, prosecuted, and stated that the prisoner, who is a widow, had for the last six months been sleeping with her children in a coal shed. She earned between 6s. and Be. a week besides her food,with washing, and it was her intemperate habits which pre- vented her from providing proper shelter for her chil- dren. She and the children were found on Monday night in a shed in Parker-st. lying on the coals without any covering whatever, and the wind sand snow were coming through a hole there was in one side of the shed. The children when found were in a filthy and half- starved condition. Dr. M`Dougall deposed to examin- ing the three children. He said he found them in an exceedingly filthy condition. There were marks upon - their bodies as if they had been very badly bitten by vermin. Although he could hardly say that they were starving it was easily seen that they did not get suffici- ent food. He had seen the shed in question,and consider- ing what a severe night it was on Monday last the circum- stance of the children sleeping there might have ended in their death.—The prisoner made no reply to the charge, but said she had done her best for her children, and could do no more.—The bench sent her to gaol for one month. with hard labour.

CHARGE AGAINST A POSTMAN.

Samuel Massey, a Frodsham letter carrier,surrendered to his ballet Cheater Assizes, on Saturday, on a charge of setting Are to his house, on the 14th August, with intent to defraud the London and Lancashire Insurance Company. It appeared that on the 27th July prisoner insured his household effects, a cow, and a pony, with the company named for £144. Not many days after- wards, namely on the night of Sunday, the 14th Aug., the prisoner's premises were found to be on fire. The house, all the doors of which were locked, was broken into, and the fire was extinguished. The facts relied upon by the prosecution to connect the prisorrer with the fire were that the fire was burning in a ceiling over a bedroom to which access could only be gained by a ladder; that a ladder was found reared up against a partition wall, which had to be scaled before the ceiling could be reached, that the prisoner was seen entering the back door leading to the loft where the ladder was found a few minutes only before the fire was discovered; and that what was found to be burning was a quantity of hay, which had to be conveyed from the place where it was usually stored, ana was evidently placed on the bedroom ceiling in small heaps. The prisoner made no claim upon the insurance company, but the prosecution suggested that he had no time for this, as within five days of the fire prisoner was in custody.--The defence Was that no motive had been shown, as the amount of the policy of insurance would not cover the value of the goods insured, that no evidence of a reliable natura pointin,-; to the prisoner's guilt had been adduced, and that to- prisoner had always borne, and still bore,a high. ,tharAc'crr. On the other hand, a police sergeant said priso:v.r had told him that the back door (the stable tor, Ce stable being under the same roof) had not been 9pened .inc,o the cow was let out in the morning,whereas a Mrs. Dinnelow saw the prisoner open and go through the door not long before the fire.—The jury acquitted the prisoner. St, George's Hall, where the ceremony took place, was packed, and in the streets through which Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone passed were very many thousands of people, who gave them an enthusiastic greeting. THE POLICE COURT CHIMNEY ON FIRE. When the last case had been heard at the Warrington PoWe Court, on Saturday, the Chairman, Mr. J. Burgess asked Chief Constable Hunt whether there was any ease of a chimney being on fire.—The Chief Constable replied that there was not.—The Chairman: There is a report that your chimitey was on fire. (Laughter.)— Mr. Hunt : I don't know of it.—The Chairman : If you inquire you will know. (Laughter.) Inspector Spinks here intormed the Bench that the police station parade room chimney had accidentally caught fire, but unless a chimney blazed out no proceedings were taken, and there was no blazing out in this case.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
_ SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Burgess (chairman), and L. Voisey.

STEALING A WAISTCOAT.—John Morgan was charged with stealing from the common lodging-house in Bank- street, on the pr...vious Tnursdav morning, a waistcoat, the property of Patrick Rooney' a ship canal labourer and a fellow-lodger. The complainant went out in the morning and on coming home at night found that both the waistcoat and the priscner had disappeared—rho prisoner : I was the worse for drink, and I thouelit it was my mate's waistcoat.—The Chairman : Then you would have Oaken the other man's waistcoat.—The prisoner: That did not matter so much.—George Hough- ton deposed to the prisoner pledging the waistcoat with him on Thursday morning and taking it out on the Friday night.—D.S.'Monagan said on his arresting the prisoner on Friday night, he admitted taking the waist- coat, but said he did not mean to steal it.—He was fined the costs, 20s. ; in default to go to jail for 7 days. DRUNK. AND DEFUSING TO QUlT—Thomas arid James Welch, brothers, were charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Higher Angel Inn the preceding, night, and James was also charged with wilfully 4, obstructing ;lie polies by attempting to rescue Thomas from custody. Mr. Critchley, the landlord, said a man named Nobby was in his house and abused and threatened " Blind Joe "who was delivering a message, the man having knocked against him. Witness told him to go out,and he refused ,and challenged witness to eject him. Witness did so, but Nobby tore his shirt, waist- coat, collar, and necktie. Thomas also refused to go out of the imose.—The constable detailed the subsequent drunken arid disorderly conduct of the two defendants in the street,and deposed to James trying to pull Thomas away from lihn.—The defendants were lined 4s. 6d. costs each. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. F. Monks (chairman), T. Pierpoint, and S. Wright. THEFTS FROM SHOPS.—James Clarke, labourer, Old road, was charged with stealing on Saturday evening, a pair of boots, value 103., the property of Mr. Jenkins 94, Bridge-st. DS. Monaghan was informed of the theft, and he found the prisoner in Mersey-st., about 8 o'clock, complaining to a constable of assault, and wearing the boots. Ile said he had bought them at a public-house for ss. and his old ones. The new boots were afterwards identified by the prosecutor—He now adhered to his statement that he had bought them. He was also charged With stealing the same morning, a slop, value is. 3d., the property of Wm. Leslie, Mersey-at. He went to Leslie7s shop, and proceeded to bargain with the hus- band for a waistcoat. He put a slop on and did not pay for it, and on Mr. Leslie leaving his wife to deal with him told her he had paid her husband. He went away with the slop on, and said he would come back about the waistcoat.— rhe prisoner said he had paid for the slop. —He was, sent to jail for three months with hard labour. THREATENING HIS WlFE—Peter Farrell, labourer, Irlam's Yard, was charged with threatening his wife, Bridget Farrell, employed at Cockhedge Factory. He was bound over in £.5 to keep the peace, and had to pay costs, in default a month's imprisonment. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Ingram Leister, file cutter, In Tilley-st., was fined 55. He had had to be driven home in his cab. He was fined ss. and costs. Fuarous Dmvusci.—Walter Bradshaw, butcher's assistant, 13. The horse had started off while he was haying a cup of coffee in the Coffee Tavern. He was fined ss. and costs. CanatzEY ON FIRE.—Wm. , 'Crossley-at. WEDNESDAY. —Rehre Mr. J. Geddes (in the chair), Councillor Fleming and Messrs. J. Fairclough and ii. Wright. EIHSBAND NOT WANTED.—Williaro Dumbell was charged with assaulting his wife Ellen Dumbell on December sth, zat the prosecutrix's house in Greenall-street. The evid- ence showed that defendant was prosecutria's husband, Ibut had been separated from her in accordance with a ,mutual agreement. On the sth of this month defendant -went to his wife's house and demanded that a writing- -desk and a portrait should be given to him. HIS wife -refused, and defendant pushed his way into the house and in doing so struck his wife.—Bound over in the slim - of £lO to keep the peace for six months. Then he gave Kenny his reward, and sent him to Strangeways to await escort. AN IxconntonstE BOY.—John Jones, of Gladstone-St., • was summoned for neglecting to send his son to school. —Defendant, in answer to Mr: Geerge Riley, admitted • that the boy had been very incorrigible, and he had at- • tempted many remedies.
