div.p: RUGBY.

, OLD Boys v. RUNCORN.—The Old Boys made the jpurney to Runcorn on Saturday, and the home organ- isation being weakened :by absence of players who were assisting the county, were helped out of the diffi- culty by New Brighton players, who had an off day. The opening passages were fairly even, the Old Boys' forward play being a very conspicuons feature. Drink- water opened the scoring account by running in a neat try, which was however, not improved upon, and following the drop out Legge looked like getting on even footing, but was firmly held. Packs resulted in the Runcornians taking the ball to the visitors' end. , Shortly following this Luva put in a grand run, and scored, but again place kicking was a failure. The play now became very fast and exciting. Herbert Woods put in several neat runs, but was unable to get fairly away,and the interval arrived without anything further being done. Riley re-started, and, after the exchanges, Luya dribbled splendidly, a movement which was imit- ated by the Boys' forwards with better results, for Wilson ran in a try and Wood kicked an unmistakeable goal. Runcorn being now behind hy a point played up for all they were worth, and were rewarded by Luya running in a further try, but before the Close Herbert Wood again gave his side the lead, and at the close of the game the scose stood—Old Boys,l goal and 1 try (7 points) ; Runcorn, 3 tries (6 points). RUNCORN RANGERS T. STOCKTON fIEA'TH. Stockton Heath, through some cause entirely unaccounted for, and which ought certainiy to be explained, failed to put in an appearance at Runcorn on Saturday ; consequently the above match was not played. WIDNES v. TUBBROOK.—At Widnes. Holmes kicked off, and in the first minute Wright scored a try for Wid- nes, and before the interval gained a second point, from which Alford kicked a goal. Half-time score—Widnes, 7 points ; Tuebrook nil. The home team had the best of the play in the second half, but failed to augment their score. Final—Widnes, 1 goall try (7 points) ; Tuebrook nil.
WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.

div.head: CUP COMPETITION.
div.p: THE CUP COMPETITION.

This was the first meeting of the teams in the Lanca- shire Cup Competition, and as both clubs occupied a good position on the list, the game was marked as being ; one of the most important in Itligby club circles. There was not the usual Warrington and Wigan crowd, and this fact is due to the nen-running of special trains from the colliery borcugh,precautions being thus taken against affording an opportunity of inducing a large number of persons to visit our infected area. Several prominent players were away from both sides, arid wh, n the teams turned up at three o'clock there would probably be a gate bordering on 5,000. Turner started towards the railway goal with a slight breeze behind him. Excite, ment was quickly roused when it was seen that the Warrington star was early in the ascendent, and after Jolley and Evans had demonstrated their usefulness, a scrimmage was formed under the Wigan posts. No sooner had the sets of forwards got their heads down than the oval carne into the possession of John Bate, and Mitchinson and Halliwell were both laiffied, an easy try being obtained. The place kick was simple enough, but Evans found it too difficult. Evans was again promin- ent soon after the drop-out, and Turner, Ash- ton and Handles supplemented the effort with a short rush which again brought troubles to Singleton's charge. Atkinson and Knowles dribbled to half-way, and in like manner Evans responded only to Singleton snap up the oval from his feet, and a fine punt reached Boscow. The latter readily piloted back, Knowles this time making his mark. I similar favour fell to Wallwork, and the visiting forwards taking advantage of a quick follow up, reached the Warrington quarters for the first time. The tattack was persisted in for a brief period, until the homesters screwed a scrim- mage finely, and Heesom, Web,ter, and Evans assisting by passing, the Wigan goal was again in jeopardy. Lawless staved off an attempt to clear, Berry, Donohue, and Homes were conspicuous parties in one fine rush. Boscow and Singleton were both applauded for a fine display of exchange kicking, whilst Ashton and Hamp- son came away from the ruck, and Wall work stepped in the nick of time, sending the oval in touch ten yards from the line. Once more Wigan cleared, this time Webster doing the trick, whilst a pretty paging move- ment by llalliwell, Mitchinson, and Knowles saw Webster tackling Wallwork, the latter incident causing much laughter, the rivals being of such unequal pro- portions. Wigan were hereabouts penalized, and Singleton meeting Turner's kick found Boscow a task which he smartly accomplished, and the Wigan cus- todian again being pressed had his frick charged, and Bate and Thornily taking the oval across the border the latter scored, but Randle s made a sorry exhibition with the place. The disappointment in the place- kicking apparently had the tendency to infuse mere spirit in the Wigan play, for on the drop-out a hasty visit was paid to the Warrington end. Ashton, Bate, and Jolley quickly followed the venue, and from a line-out Singleton saved, a perform- ance he repeated a few moments later from some clever work by Lawless. Singleton and Webster next ex- changed, the latter coming off with honours, and Berry being smart in following was almost a scorer, Carmody saving well. Turner made a fine effort from a line-out, but held the oval a trifle too long, and as a result the visitors got the oval away to half-way. Webster was soon forcing a way through the thick of his opponents, Wallwork and a host of his companions pulling up the Warringtonian. A fine rush by the Wigan forwards was responded to by the local nine, and following this came another spell of exchange kicking, Webster sending up the third minor. The homesters still maintained their aggressive tactics, and Singleton having a kick charged by Hampson, the oval was eventually taken over by ' Heesom, and Webster set his predecessors an example by kicking a neat goal. The leaders maintained their posi- tion right up to the interval, when they led by a goal, two tries, three minors to nil. On resuming, the locals again assumed a threatening attitude, and Singleton only just cleared his charge. Berry, Donohue, and Jolley had the visitors back on their lines, but some ex- cellent forward play by the whole array of the Wiganers resulted in the game being waged near the home posts. The Wigan backs failed to utilize chances, Carmody fail- ing signally at one attempt, and profiting by the latter's failure, Lawless rushed along, being pulled down when half way had been passed. A mull by a homester led up to Wigan attacking, and five'minutes were spent in stiff scrimmaging on the home lines, Donohue dribbled out of danger, and Boscow improved tho homesters' position in replying to Knowles' kick. The visitors still continued to have the best of the deal, but darkness coming on it was with difficulty that the players were distinguished. Wigan pressed once more, and Berry dribbled out of danger, Lawless putting in a fine run, which elicited loud cheers. From a long kick Boscow saved, and a temporary cessation was caused by Atkinson, the Wigan skipper, being seized with a fit, due to excitement. From what could be gleaned of the play from this paint War- rington had a little the best of it, Jolley and Handles almost getting in. The end soon came and Warring,ten sent up their third win in the csmpetition, the score of the day's play reading—Warrington, 1-2-4 : Wigan, 0-0-1. Teams :—J. Boscow, back ; H. Webster, y. Heesom, and P. R. Lawless, three-quarters ; John Bate and John Evans, half backs; H. Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Randles, 'l'. Donohue, W. Berry, G. Hampson, J. Holmes, and J. T. Thorniley, forwards. , Wigan : Singleton, back ;A. Wallworth, A. Knowles, and R. Carmody, three-quarters ; W. Halliwell, and J. Mitchinson, half backs ; W. Atkinson (captain), E. Wardle, W. Unsworth, Prescott, WlNTarnara, Webster, Fairclough, Grundy, and Bennerson, forwards. Mr. E. H. Flower, of Broughton, officiated as referee. JUNIOR LEAGUE.

WARRINGTONJVIORS v. WARTUNOTON RANCIHRS. The return match betwet n the above teams rook place on the ground of the former. Two twenties being arranged, the Juniors kicked off, the ball going in touch. From the line out, the Rangers took the game in the home quarters, where from a combined dribble, Broad- hurst secured an unimproved try. Upon the drop out the Rangers still kept up the pressure, and from a scrimmage near the line, Clarke skipped round the pack and placed a second try to his side's account. These early successes of the Rangers seemed to discourage theik opponents, one of whom, for some infringement,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 10. 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 10. 1892.

was ordered off the field. The Juniors' captain made matters worse by refusing to proceed with the game,and the match terminated after twelve minutes' play, the score at the time being Rangers, two tries; Juniors, nil. Referee, Mr. W. Speakman, W. F. C. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH v. LATCHFORD 1113CRHA- TION.—The above teams met on Saturday in the junior competition. The homesters from various causes mus- tered but poorly, no less than five reserves having to be called upon. The Parish started operations, and it was not long before their forwards, combining well, gained a footing in the Recs. • quarter. A pretty display of pass- ing saw Carey giving Welsby a beautiful chance, and the first try was scored. The drop out gave the visitors no relief, for although they had they had the advantage so far as weight was concerned, there was no show of combination, and as the result of a series of scrimmages on the visitors' lines, Garrity secured and dodged over. The call of half time found the score unaltered, the home team leading by two tries. The resumption was the opening up of good play which resulted it the Parish Church augmenting their score to five tries, whilst that of the Latchford Recs. remained as before— nil.

div.head: MAKING OF PRIVATE STREETS.
div.p: THE MAKING OF PRIVATE STREETS.
RELIEF FOR PROPERTY OWNERS.

At a meeting of the 'sown Council,on Tuesday night, Councillor Henry Roberts submitted the fol- lowing motion :—`• That it be an instruction to the Finance Committee as and from March 25th next to declare the expenses incurred in the making of pri- vate streets, whenever a majority of the owners of the properties abutting on such streets may desire it,to be private improvement expenses,and to make such arrangements as may be necessary for allow- ing tc the owners of the property referred to a period not exceeding five years for the payment of their apportionments of the cost of such private improvements." In doing so he said it would be within the recollection of the members that a simi- lar resolution was adopted by a unanimous vote of the Council a couple of years ago, requesting the Paving and Sewerage Committee to report on the principle involved in the present resolution. The committee found, however, that it was not a matter which concerned them, but more, the Finance Com- mittee. The resolution, if carried, would throw the onus on the Finance Committee of making arrange- ments for the collection of the money involved in the cost of street making, and on those grounds the matter was referred to the Finance Committee. On that occasion the Finance Committee did not see their way to adopt the principle. Two years had since elapsed, and during that period he had good reason for stating that there I had been a considerable change of opinion both inside and outside the Council. The only serious objections which were raised against the resolution at the period of which he spoke could be condensed into two, and were shortly that no man had a right to commence building operations until he had possession cf funds wherewith to meet every obligation. Such an argument was utterly indefensible. There were not above four or Ave per cent, of the people in Warrington and neighbour- hood who could have started on the erection of build- ings had they been compelled to meet every obligation in the first instance ; and had it not been for the advant- ages offered by the different building societies in the town to enable industrious workmen to save a little money, and become through their medium owners of property in which they resided, there would have been fewer property owners that day. (Hear, hear.) He contended that the sooner they recognized the principle of offering facilities to people for erecting buildings the better would it be for the town. The erection of pro- perty tended to make the town more prosperous. The only other serious objection made was in regard to the increased book-keeping. Re questioned very much the worth of sad' an argument. The Corporation would incur no risk whatever, and in support of his argument he cited as an illustration the adoption of the principle in other towns, and further, the Cor- poration were protected, inasmuch as they had the first charge on the property concerned.— Alderman WRIGET suggested that Councillor Roberts should limit his term for repayment to three years in- stead of five. (Hear, hear.) The Council ought not to allow such an extended credit.—Councillor SHAW GREEN, in seconding the adoption of the motion, said that the Council ought to do everything that was possible to in- duce building operations. The Public Health Act even suggested that time should be allowed for the repay- ment of the cost of the pavement of streets. Continu- ing, Councillor Green quoted as an instance the success of the adoption of the principle in Richmond. The Treasurer of the Local Authority had remarked at a con- ference recently held that the scheme had encouraged building operations in the jurisdiction of the Board.. Further, the enormous sum of £20,000 was actually owing to the Board in regard to street improvements. —ln reply to Councillor Monks, Alderman WRIGHT remarked that the paving of a street in front of a cot- tage was about £9 on the average.—Councillor SET- BURST pointed out that there were over 2,000 people connected with various building societies in the town who had built houses, and it seemed to him that the re- payment of is. a week in respect of street paving would come heavily on them. On that ground he thought the five years' limit was quite small enough. (Hear, hear.) —Alderman HOLMES said his opinion was that noman hal a right to enter into building speculations unless he was prepared with the cost beforehand. (Hear, hear.) The principle suggested by Councillor Roberts was only encouraging the leaving over until the morrow what should be met at once. He was certain that the Finance Committee would not entertain a period of five years. Three years was quite long enough in his estimation. —Councillor MONKS opposed the motion on the grounds that it would only encourage the building of jerry pro- perty, and lead persons to undertake the erection off pro- perty who were really unable to meet the demands upon their capital. Respecting the Building Societies which had been alluded to, he could only remark that he was not at all in favour of them. He considered they were to a certain extent gambling institutions— for it was what the speculation amounted to-; and he looked upon them with suspicion. He wanted to, know if it was not as fair for the Corporption to help a, manu- facturer in erecting his works, as it was to help a man in building his house.—Councillor ROBERTS, in replying, characterised Councillor Monks's objections as absurd, and respecting his question as to the claim a manufac- turer had on the Corporation, he said it was a thought- lesss interrogation. Anyone knew that, comparatively speaking, a cottager contributed much more to,therates than any manufacturer, and was in every possible man- ner justified in asking for more assistance from the Cor- poration than a manufacturer was. In conchisine, he consented to alter the term of credit to threelears.— The motion was then carried.

div.head: "LANCASHIRE LADS" FOR INDIA.
div.p: "LANCASHIRE LADS" FOR INDIA.

The King's Own Royal Lancaster Regiment sent a draft, undhr Captain Barton, of four subalterns and 150 rank and tile to India by the Enphrates, which left Portsmouth on Wednesday. The draft joins the 2nd Battalion headquarters at Ahmed muggiar, to which place all letters should be addressed, and is the best,per- haps, the King's Owia has sent out for years. All the men have boen through an Aldershot season, where the " little Lancaster men "marched with a swing and en- durance that would have done credit to much older men.

div.head: "EAWR CHARLIE'S GONE V'
div.p: "EAWR CHARLIE'S GONE V'

My chums, wo luv a faithful pup, Come in wi' me, and hey a sup, An' help me 't keep my sperrits up— Eaur Charlie's gone ! To' moant make gammon o' my grief, But help me to some stnaw relief, For ov aw dogs he ems the chief— Eaur Charlie's gone ! Fro hares an' rappits he knock'd spots, An' cats he dubbl et up i' knots, While he wur gradely rough on rots ! Eaur Charlie's gone! Like some good Christians, he wed feight Wi' pugs an' tarsiers twice his weight; But, Lord I if he's made sossige meyt ! Baur Charlie's gone ! Sumtimes he'd gantle off at neet, An' if he met a sweetheart reet, We miss'd him then till mornin' leet—

Eaur Charlie's gone ! But that's a trick that ev'n a lad, If he'd tan up a coortin' fad, Wud do just same, an' be BS glad— Eaur Charlie's gone ! Wot will th' owd station master say, Wen he finds eaut he's slipt away? He'll mebbe coss,—he'll never pray ! Coze Charlie's gcne! He wanted me—that best.' men— To hey his ears mark'd wi' a enn, So we cud trace the divil then—

- But Charlie's gone! An' neaw he'll hardly speyk to me ; But wi' a twinkle in his e'e, He'll sheaut, wi' snetrin' grim an'dree„ " Ez Charlie gone?" Air connot stolid that raspin' text; But woteoever he sez next, Aw'll only smile—aw'll not get vext, Fer Charlie's gone ! If in th' Hotel, he'll meet me theer, th' Paper Manager i h' cheer, We'll Berry avr before di' New Year, Fer Charlie's gone ! An' then, wen thus we'n clear'd the greaund„ An' cum to raison safe an' seaun -1, We'll drink Good Health i' whiskies reaund, Tho' Charlie's gone! TUM 0' PEGS. Rose Bonk, December 9, 1892.
INSPECTOR RILEY'S ADVENTURE.
HE IS IN "FEAR OF HIS LIFE."

It is well known that the duties of School At- tendance Officer Riley are often invested with snore genuine excitement than enjoyable pleasure. The wealth of abuse which he receives from his 'patients," is often only equivalent to the extent of his own wealth of geniality. He met with an adventure on Wedneselay.. As he was proceeding along Knutsford-road, he was Accosted by a con- spicuously wull built female named Mrs. Elizabeth Harris. She stood at the corner of York-st., and informed Mr. Riley of her intention to hit him, on Recount of saying " nasty things" about her at St. Mary's Roman Catholic schools. " Madam, I as- sure you I never said any such. thing," said the Inspec- tor, "and if you will come wittrtne to the school I will prove. it." So she went with him. Be commenced to ad- duce his proof, bat by-and-by the irate lady said she would give him proof. She woad give him proof of her pugilistic powers; and she dropped her basket and "- banged "at him ; but the blow missed. And, after this she couldn't hit him, simply because he climbed over some forms. Be then tried to leave rapidly,. not out of mere " matter of form, " so much as out of pressing necessity. Before he left the building,however, Mrs. Harris had directed language at him of a more forcible than polite nature, and she concluded by stating that she and her husband would visit him at his lodgings and "lam him well. The school attendance officer told the Bench on Thursday that he had been in a depressed state since, and as the legal phrase has it, "was in: fear of his life." Mrs. Barris tried to,explain to the same Bench her anxiety to thrash the officer,, but it only ended in her being pound over to keep the peace for, six months. The Chief Constable remarked that Mr.. Raley and his assistants often complained of similar abuse, and he thought the police would have to take rigid,steps to put it down.

div.head: LABOTTCHERE: AND THE " DAILY NEWS."
div.p: LABOTTCHERE: AND THE " DAILY NEWS."
RUMOURED NEW RADICAL, JOURNAL.

Since there is no longer any concealment necessary with regard. to the severance of Mr. Labouchere's con- nection with. the" Daily News," I may mention, says a London correspondent, that the price paid for his share in the newspaper was 00,000: When he first became connected with the proprietorship of the paper, more than five and twenty years ago, he nsrld the representa- tives of the•outgoing or deceased shareholder £ll,OOO, for the holding of which he has now received a sum more than sufficient to start a morning newspaper of his own. Nothing is yet known as to his intentions, but it is regarded as.by no means i:npossible that, in conjunction with Sir Charles Dilke, who has long wished to own or have an interest in a daily paper, some plan may be adopted by which the advanced or disaffected Radicals, as distinguished from the Ministerialists, will have an organ of their own.

div.head: REPORTED ILLNESS OF MRS. MAYBRICK.
div.p: THE REPORTED ILLNESS OF MRS. MAYBRICK.

The Governor of Woking Prison, telegraphing to the Presa•Association regarding the reported serious illness of Mrs. Maybrick„ says he can. give no information without authority. The Press Asse,ciation Woking correspondent tele- graphs that Mrs. Maybrick has. been in the hospital for the past ten months suffering from general debility, which culminated some weeks ago in hemor-bage of. the lungs. On Monday she became worse, and at her 'request the last sacraments 04 the olureh of England were administened. Since then her condition has re- mained precarious, and her =other, who was sent for, saw Mrs. Maybrick on Tuesday. (INTERVIEW WITH THE B&RONESS VON ROQUES . . .

- In a later telegram, the Press Association's Woking correspondent says he has had an interview with the Baroness von, Rogues, who is remaining In theleigh- bourhood,,imthe hope of being allowed to see the patient again in the event of a fatal turn of the malady. She expressed absolute belief in the prisoner's innocence,and a lingering hope that the eling of the English people may lead to her release. In that event, added the baroness,. they could spend together the short period of life that semains to her daughter.

Nearly two thousand men out of employment marched through the streets of Glasgow on Thursday, and dis- played banners on which they demanded justice instead of charity, overwork for none, and week for all. An open-air meeting was held, and a deputation chosen by the men afterwards waited on the magistrates. It was explained to the unemployed that relief works had been opened at the new public park for the city, and that work could be obtained there.

div.head: DRUNKEN. ORGIE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: A DRUNKEN. ORGIE AT ST. HELENS.
"WAKING A CORPSE."

THE HOUSE ON FIRE.—EXCITING SCENE. The particular part of St. • Helens in which desti- tution and squalor are rampant is, says the Liver- pool " Daily Post," inappropriately called Green- bank, and in it an exciting incident occurred in the early hours 0 Sunday morning. Fifty or sixty years since the district which lies off Liverpool- road, was charmingly picturesque, but now huge towers and sheds and chimneys of chemical works crown its height, and under their shadows are a num- ber of streets in which a good many Irish families " exist." Scores of houses are dilapidated, and the "sticks "which do duty for furniture are of such a quality that no respectable artisan would carry them home for firewood. Our correspondent has on mcre than one occasion visited the neighbourhood, and wit- nessed the most appalling destitution. Two or more families occupy one house—one set of inmates con- nected by ties of relationship having the two front rooms and another family at the back part. Some can boast a ricketty table and an old chair,but in some instances the mother may be seen sitting on an old soap-box trying to warm herself by an almost fireless grate, and the chil- dren scattered up and down the flbor. 4lt to bed- ding there is little or none, and frequently an old straw mattress on the floor, where fathers and mothers and little ones •lie together, generally in their apology for clothes, is the substitute. In one of the thoroughfares mentioned—viz., in John-street--an old man and woman recently came and took a house,. but their belongings were of the most scanty description. The m4n came to be known as " Old Pat 4an '"— whether that was his proper name, no oue knew—and 1 ' he eked out a scanty existence for himself and his wife by gathering raga and banes and by a small allowance from the parish. On Friday night or Saturday morning he died, and the parish officers, in the interests of health and propriety,. fixed Sunday for the funeral. On Saturday the plain coffin arrived, and the body, placed therein, was carried from the coverless bed on which hehad died, and placed on trestles in the front room below. The" sorrow " , took the form of the usual wake, and although no money could be found for the last sad obsequies to be done •"' decently and in order," neighbours were not slow to, provide funds for drink. On Saturday night the candles were lighted, and a number of persons—one informant described /ran of the motley crowd as balf-a-dozen youtha and girls—visited and remained in the house. . The widow was also regaled, and after her " friends " had retired she managed to get upstairs, and threw her- self maim the old mattress on which her husband died. kbout roust:Mock an alarm was raised that the house was on fire,. and smoke was plainly seen to be issuing , from the windows. Several neighbours broke in, and on going upstairs they found the mattress on fire, and the old' woman too stupefied to do anything to safe herself. The window could not be opened, so the panes were broken to let the smoke out and the fresh air in. Then. she was carr'ed downstairs, and buckets of water were thrown. upon the smouldering straw. The neighbour- hood was soon in a state of great alarm, and the police . came hurrying up to render assi4tance, which they did ,effectually. The Fire Brigade were also apprised of the , occurrence, widowersl members, under Superintendent 1 Bychall, ran to the plaCe. How the fire originated is ' not known. The water from the buckets saturated the libor, and fell upon the coffin of thedead husband below. Another informant says r.--.." The fire brigade were called out a few, minutes after four o'clock, but when they arrived on the M 4113 the finished been put out. Super- ihtendent Birdie!! and Sergeant Penketti went into the house. What first met their view was the coffin, of which they had no knowledge, and this did not cense them a pleasant sensation. They went upstairs, and saw the mattress which had been burned. The bedstocks were in the corner,. and the only other furniture in the . room.was the framework of what had once been a rush- bottom chair, with,a piece of wood over the seat. The water.had been thrown, over the bed and had dripped through the flbor on to the corpse below. There were three. brass Candlestick, with lighted candles, indicat- ing that something. in thenature of a wake had been going on. Seeing that everything was safe, and that there was no likelihood of any further outbreak, the brigade left." Duriiia Sunday morning the widow recovered from the effects of' her fright and narrow escape, and the body other husband was taken away and placed in a grave at St. Efelens Cemetery by the parish officials.

THE COLLAPSE OF THE SAGE OF PENKETH. Sir,—Not for one moment did I suspect that the "state of the moon "had anything to do in influencing the Sage of Penketh. In the si nplicity of nature, such a suspicion never crossed my mind. It is needless to say that, had I known of it, never, for one moment,should I have discussed the matter with him, but would gladly have left him, while under the chilling influences of the pale moonbeams, to indvlge in poetic effusions to his heart's content, and in composing " shady latinity " to inscribe on dead men's tombstones.—Yours, &c. Dec. sth, 1892.
A LEARNER.

THE EPIDEMIC.—PRACTICAL OBSERVATIONS. Sir,—Now that the abatement in the epidemic has allayed public uneasiness, it will not be out of place to make a few commonplace remarks on the occurrences of the past few weeks. I do not write as an anti- vaccinator, which I am not, but as one who has taken an interest, and has studied in the subject more closely perhaps than the majority of work-a-day people. Vaccination,as at present regulated by law,is admitted- ly incomplete, and that it has failed to prevent our epidemic of smallpox is self-apparent. When the epidemic began there was not a single cry raised that the town was not well vaccinated. It could not be so, when such men as Mr. Robert Davies repudiated in pub- lic the assertion of Mr. Harry Furniss that it was other- wise; and still more pointedly Mr. Sutton, clerk to the Beard of Guardians, at the meeting of that body on Wednesday, said that the ordinary vaccination fee pay- able to the public vaccinator for every case of "successful" vaccination was Is 6d, but when the Government Official considered the duties well done he recommended an additional fee. It speaks well for our public vaccinator that this additional fee has always been recommended and paid him. But the very fact of this premium being paid brings us face to face with the fact that Warrington was a well vaccinated town, and I yet that smallpox obtained an extraordinary hold. The pertinacity with which each death of an un- vaccinated person has been recorded has been very obvious, and it behoves the public to enquire into the circumstances of a few of -these. One or two will suffice to show how frail are the grounds upon which. is based the implied assumption that these were solely due to non-vaccination. Example 1: The tramp with whom the epidemic began, belonging to a class peculiar- ly susceptible of catching, retaining, and developing any disease in his body goes about unattended, until the fatal symptons are visibly far advanced upon him. Surely the death of such a man could not he attributed to non-vaccination. Example 2: A little girl left to rot and die in a bed and house of filth, suffering from neglect and the worst form of smallpox; can that death be justly attributed to non-vaccination? No. yet it helps to count. Examp'e 3: A filecutter neglects all care of himself, and actually continues his work until the marks are upon him. Here again the death was more attributable to neglect and exposure than non- vaccination, but nn account is taken on that score. Example 4 : An infant 9 clays old. As if such an infant had any chance to combat with disease of so virulent a type. This was surely drawing it too far. If one could ascertain the constitutional fitness of a person to withstand a disease reliance could be placed on such evidence as has been adduced, but when cases such as I refer to are included wholesale, then the evidence is undoubtedly weakened,because if every case of death of an unvaccinated person from smallpox were examined into there might be found equally convincing facts which would favour the growth and development of the disease independent of non-vaccination. This leads one to ask himself the following question :—" Given two cases in similar circumstances with the exception that one is vaccinated and the other is not, which of theee two would receive greater attention in a hospital at the hands of a doctor who believes in vaccination ?" Some may say that,believing in the efficacy of vaccination, the doctor would devote more attention to the patient he considered in a more dangerous condition. I may be wrong, but I rather think that he would be disposed to endeavour more earnestly to restore the vaccinated per- son, as his recovery and the death of the other would materially go to strengthen his vaccination theory and rice versa. Of worse that is only a matter of opinion, but the temptation to do so is there. The local statistics would be far more to the point if they disclosed the pro- portion of cases of dissipated or intemperate habits, to those of temperate habits, well nourished to poorly nourished, and smokers to non-smokers. Vaccination having proved a failure, re-vaccination is resorted to. We are told that if all the people in War- rington had been re-vaccinated three months ago there would not he a single case of smallpox in the town to-day. It could with far more certainty be said that if the infected tramp had been properly seen to and if there had been properly isolated accommodation, there would not only be not one, but there would not have been more than that one case of smallpox in Warrington from first to last of the present epidemic. It is unkind, unintentionally no doubt, of the medical profession to interrupt the rich harvest their co-helpers in the healing art, the chemists, are enjoying, by proclaiming that re-vaccination is a charm which conapletely puts in the shade all other safeguards, such as camphor, chloride of lime, carbolic acid, Stc.,Stc. The abatement in the epid- emic. about the progress of which, all the same, we would like more publicity, is attributed solely to re-vac- cination. Have none of the following agencies had nothing to do with it—the liberal use of disinfectants, latterly, more careful removal of patients and perhaps most important of all, the improvement in the weather from damp and fog to comparative clearness. This putting forward of re-vaccination as the only safeguard is fatal ; it may retard our already tardy enough Sanitary Committee in securing properly isolated hospital accommodation, and it has a baneful influence upon many people who, on the strength of that belief, neglect ordinary precautions. The danger arising from the operation of vaccination and re-vace.ination is a phase of the question upon which I will not dwell at length. Within my own narrow circle of acquaintances, several have been brought almost to death's door. If that is its effects on adults what will be its effects on infants ? Some idea will be gleaned from the following figures. In 1847 there were 55,135 deaths of babies under one year, (to every million of births) caused through diseases attribu- tahle in a great measure to vaccination, but in 1886 the number swelled to 84,029. In the case of syphilis alon3 which Dr. Creighton and Dr. Jonathan Hutchinson say can be conveyed by vaccine lymn,li the deaths of babies were 472 in 1847, and'lBB2 in IEB7. Thyme figures prove the danger of vaccination, and while the medicali profession, so far as they support vaccination, are almost at one in saying that the beneficial effects are lost in course of years, they are at sixes and sevens as to where re-vaccination should be resorted to. Some say s.others6,7.and on to 12. 'Flte advocates of VAMCinatiOri are thus in the peculiar position of admitting that their theory is incomplete ; and to put themselves in a logically consistent position they should be equally as energetic in agitating to make re.varcination compulsory every so many years. as the anti-vaceinatore are in agitating for the repeal of compukory vaceination. I refrain, however, from enterinl into debatable ground on this occasion, and will c•onclude by pointing 1 out that good sanitation is and never can be neutralised by plentiful vaccieation, that cleanly habits, plain Sub- stantial dietary, a healthy mind in a healthy body, are not without their infleence in epidemics of this kind. Cleanliness is not only nett' tO godlineee, but it is also 1002 way ahead of vaccination or revaccination.—Yours, " CLEO.

div.head: WATCHING THE CASES.
div.p: WATCHING THE CASES.
Al THE BOROUGH COURT.
BY LUKE BLUNT.

Yes, I had often read with mixed feelings of pity and reproach,of the poor defendants at the Borough Court. My heart had always been abundantly filled with sentiments ot pity and sympathy, for the poor dissolute man, who, after passing from quiet and respectability, through the throes of care and trouble, had at last sought the cup that inebriates to drown his sorrows, and then after making one false step, drifted into " the box." Or, may be, it was the poor,homeless boy—the nobody's child—that I thought of. The homeless, ragged, uncared for urchin, that I had seen pictured in the tract book, with matted flaxen locks, and calm, blue eyes, whose only act of criminality was stealing a penny crumpit to give temporary sustenance to his fast-ebbing life. Or it might have been the unfor- tunate widow that earned ray sympathy, for in the same tracts on the Police Court I had read of her. Iliad sobbed over the pitiful description of how she had struggled on, without parish relief, fighting against consumption and decline, and trying to bring up her little fatherless children on the pro- ceeds of the labour of her own delicate fingers ; and how,in a time of want her little Willie stayed from school, to save the school wage, and thus brought his trembling mother into the clutches of the School Attendance authorities.

It was my sympathy which led me to visit the Borough Police Court, a short time ago. I opened the door and passed into the awe-inspiring room of justice. I sat down and began to watch. Bye and by Patrick Bently Touchem'a name was called. This, I thought, was one of the poor dissolute men. Wm. was brought out and put in the box. But he was just a little disappointing, because he hadn't the Sunday School Superintendent aspect about him which I had seen in the tract. His fine muscular hands gripped the side of the dock like a vice, his eyes shone with Cie appearance of ten candle strength lamps, and as he looked at the two ad- jacent policemen he certainly impressed one with the idea that he could have blown them over like an American blizzard. But still he only lacked two things and they were: a shave and a—well, it was a shirt. He was full of feeling, was Wm. His passion for his wife had been so strong that she wished it to be weakened a little. He had cues/led her cheeks with the fireirons, and attempted to smooth down her auburn locks witt the coal hammer. Once he saved her the expense of buying rouge by tinting her face with a gentle touch of the soft hand which had thrown her out of the window. He denied the assault, and said he was as innocent as a babe un- born. He was asked if he wanted to ask his wife any questions, so he said „. . . . . .

"Shure oi do." (Then turning with a pleading look to his wife) " Betty me darlint, and did ye say oi give ye that black oye. Now spake the truth, me dear—me only guiding star." Then he gave her a look full of deep, melancholy, and martyr-like affection.
"Ye give me both of 'em, and ye struck me wid a poker last week, too. Yer a nasthy spalpeen." . . .

. . "Oh (piously') me poor losht pet'! I 'liver did such a ting, Betty, ye know it darlint. Betty, ye moind whin yer was ill, how kmnd and tinder oi was. Ye remember how oi come home at night,and narsed little bloikey. Oh, darlint, ye moind too. that it was myself that paid for the whiskey and snuff at yer poor, dead, father's wake. Yer moind--"
"Now Patrick you must only ask her questions," interposes one of the officers persuasively. " All-a-roight. Betty did oi hit ye wid that poker.?".

" " May heaven forgive her, gintlemen, for she bloights her tinder husband's life wid a big, sinful, loie. She'l think of her moighty cruelty whin oi loi in the cold, dark, cells, wid a breaking heart— she'l rnoind these falling tears thin—" "Ask questions, sir," said one of the officers fiercely. " Arra! Who are ye to to be orthering me about. Kape yur place sur, yer but a placeman. Oim the son ov me own dead father, Patrick Bentley Touchem, and as good a man as ye." " Do you want to ask any more questions?." in- terposes the magistrate's clerk. " Oil not answer to plase ye ! " "Then you can sit down Mrs. Touchem." " But oi want her to stand up sor, and stand up she will."
"Just hold your chattering tongue sir," exclaimed the Chairman angrily. " Fwhat ! carn't oi do what oi plase wid me own woife, now ? "

"No sir, you cannot" bawled the magistrate, "and you must go to prison for one month for doing what you have done." William ee-med considerably disconcerted at this decision, and so did his wife. She instantly broke out into tears and pleaded that he might not be sent to jail. Indeed, she said she'd let lisr husband "do it again," if they would only let him go. And they let him go ; but it was only down to the cells. I was a bit disappointed at this, but when I saw Mr. Riley get up and call out a name, I looked eagerly for the seedy, genteel, consumptive widow, dressed in widow's weeds. But she didn't come, somehow. It was another woman, a big, tall, stout matron with an aspect of considerable fierceness about her eyes ; something which reminded one of a double-edged meat axe. When Mr. Riley spoke of her boy missing school 70 times out of 100, she just set too with her story. She said : " Mr. Rilem. I should like to speak to you. I want to know what right you had for to send me that post card—l've getten it here "Your Plenerey's attendants at skoo is wery unsatisfactory. If he doesn't attend more regularly proceeds will be takken agen 'im—Yourn trooly George Rilem." They will, will they. Now Rilem, look me in the eyes and see if there's green theere. What did you sent that card for; to let the postman know all our business! Its scandaleous it is. Umph ! And about my Jon Henerey, too, as though he wasn't all right. He's received a proper business education as will help him, as my Jon Henerey. There ain't a handier lad anywhere for selling papers and matches and carrying parcels. And he can read like—Well, come here and show 'em Jon Henerey. This is th' book (In a whisper: Read what tha's been practicing about the horses.) John Henry, turning up a marked page : " Opon a time a neighing steed Who grazed among a numerous breed, 'With—wi— Why this isn't the one mover P Mr. Riley : Gentlemen, I'm disgusted with this nonsense. This is one of my worse cases and I ask for the full penalty. John Henerey's mother said : " Oh:! Rilan ! Well I donno."

_ The Chairman: That boy has not passed his stan- dards and he is not 13 yet, and with the full know- ledge of this you have transgressed the law. An order will be made for your boy's return to school, and you will be fined 2s. 6d. and costs. The old matron was hurried out of the court and Mrs. llamhone was called. She came along presently leading a little girl, whose face was enswarthed with a piece of red flannel. Mr. Riley was fiery now, and having glanced once at the party to see that it was the right one, he wtnt on to tell the Bench bow that child with the red flannel had only been to school 48 times during the past ten weeks, only 48—no more, no less—just simply 48. It was scandelous. And there was nothing the matter with the girl. " Oh ! aint there?" and Mrs. Hambone fixed Mr. Riley with a steady, strong, gaze. "She was told by her teacher that she was too ill to go, now then.' " Here Elizabeth," :.aid the Chairman to the child "What have you got that flannel on your head for?" " I've got the toofake, sir" said she shyly, but looking considerably bright and happy under the affliction. -
"How long have you had it? Since yesterday ?" sail thrk Chairman coaxingly, for the mother said Elizabeth had suffered for three months.

The child hesitated ; thc ache said " Yes ! 'mean I --I—l. It's ached for free hours." "Oh !" ejaculated the Chairman. " I think you will have to pay a fine of 2s. 61. Mrs. Hambone." Having made the uAual speech, and thrown the 4cust,.inBry dark scowl at Mr. Riley, the good lady id and went. I left in a short time, generally disappointed with the unpleasant shock which my sympathies had received, Air I bad seen not one of my much wept-over, unfortunate specimens of humanity presented to me in the tract book.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL. Peformances were renewed on the Warrington P.C. field on the Causeway on Saturday. Our home' boys" for the first time in a fortnight donned their short pants and jerseys, and struck another blow for the Lancashire Rugby Cup.

Their opponents were Wigan, and the two clubs met for the first time since the organisation of a Lancashire Cup Competition, and when they parted, after the game, some few Wigan men, of an unpersistent character, even expressed the hope that they wouldn't meet Warrington again in the competition. Perhaps it's just as well, if they are at all ambitious to win the cup ! Warrington parted from them with a score of 1-2-4 to 0-0-4. This places our home team on an equality with St. Helens Recs. in the competition. Swinton are leaning with five wins and no lesses,and Warrington and St. Helens follow up next. Broughton, Oldham, and Broughton Rangers are snugly nestling together, and apparently competing for the last place on the list. 'lhey have all played eight matches, of which they have won one each.

Before the ball had been rolling two minutes, the strange, hoarse surging roar, which floats on the breeze from the football field when Warrington are doing "the trick," was to be heard. Late visitors ran post haste down the causeway, heeding nothing in the way of puddles and slough, and having scampered into the fled, arrived in time to learn that John Bate had put the leather over the line. And immediately after the throw- out Thornily went and did just the very same thing. The spectators liked this playful mimicry, but Wigan people didn't seem to appreciate it.

Boscow was there in all the resplendent glory of his county jersey, and when he made his appearance on the field at the commencement of the game, he was loudly applauded. He played well all through his performances. being safe and steady. Aboht the grand stand the full backs' play against Yorkshire the previous week, was freely commented upon, and the general opinion ex- pressed tallied with that of Captain Ashton, made through the columns of the Ea-arainer last week.

The game, looking at it all round, was a good one, hut decidedly one-sided, for during the whole of the first half the visitors were constantly struggling beneath their own posts. Indeed, when, by a little deserving merit they dicl get the ball on to Warrington territory, Lengthy Webster discouraged them by putting into effect his long kicks and sending the ball back again. , He did this often, and once, just when a little Wigan man named Wallwork, was going to score, tall Mr. Webster wouldn't let him try (!), and snatched the ball from him and ran away. Aud people laughed at little Wallwork, because Webster put his big legs over his head.

Towards the close of the second half the visitors plucked up a little courage, and Warrington lost a little. The ball came dangerously often on to Warring- ton ground, and several times had the visitors had a little pressure behind them, their chances would have been considerably safe. It was on these occasions that Boscow showed the value and reliability of his play. Bate, Evans, Hampson, Jolley and Donohue all gave noticeably good performances too.

One noticeable point about the match was the absence of the monotonous forward play, which has generally been associated with Wigan. To the credit of the whole team it must be said that they discarded all their old methods, and played an exceedingly good Rugby game.

Another noticeable point in the game was of a less en- joyable nature. The game was brought to a temporary cessation owing to an accident to Atkinson, the visitors' captain. After entering a rush, he suddenly fell down. Some said he was in a fit, and others said he was "only winded !" For a time he was treated for both of these, until, fortunately, a member of the Y.M.C.A. ambu- lance class came along. He discovered that he was suffering from slight concussion of the brain, owing to a knock. Ile revived him and then had him conveyed to the Roe Buck Inn. This certainly reflects some credit upon the Y.M.C. A. class.

Cumberland are likely to meet Yorkshire. Middlesex, &c„ and then they will be better tested than they have been so far in the corapetition. A year ago it would have been any odds you like to name on either of the counties named beating the Cumbrlans, but now the latter have got their backs up, so to speak, and will con- sequently go into the struggles with a vast deal more confidence and triumph.

What a rare set-to that will be between Yorkshire and Middlesex, and what agate there will be if the match comes off in the West Riding! For ourselves we should not like to see Yorkshire win the championship this year. It is becoming a trifle monotonous to see it go so often to the broad-acred county, and it is time someone else bad a look in.

Cheshire were not eliciting loud outbursts of applause from the spectators at Durham last Saturday. I can't exactly say what the reason was, but a sporting paper says the Cestrians were scarcely ever in it with Alder- son's fifteen, and but for Houghton's brilliant defence a big score would have been piled up against them.

div.p: 1,418 C ELL ANSOU 8 .

During the past fortnight the attendances at the " Gym" have gone up 20 per cent., which is pro- bably accounted for by the decrease in the smallpox scare, and the recovery of the members from the effects ef vaccination. It hio not yet been settled whether the home team will meet the Birmingham "Gym." away during the competition, or at home. I heard this week that the Committee are contemplating the opening of the fortnightly displays, and that the first entertain- ment is likely to take place m.rly next month.

Since its removal to Palmyra Square the "Gym." can flatter itself upon having gained a considerable amount of celebrity in the gymnastic world. It is going on the right way to increase this, for I believe the Committee have now turned their attention to the organisation of a new branch to be held its connection with the Irish National League.

div.head: LY MM.
div.p: LY MM.

ANNUAL MRETINO OP THE LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The annual meeting of the Lymm rolling District Liberal Association was held in the Club-room, Eagle Brow, on Monday night, Mr. J. A. Swanwick in the chair. Mr. John itylands, Thelwall, was unanimously re-elected president, Mr. J. A. Swanwick chairman, Mr. G. L. Welford treasurer, and Mr. W. Skilling, secretary. Twenty-seven delegates were elected to represent the association at the meetings of the Altrincham Division Liberal Association. The treasurer submitted a state- ment of accounts for the past year, which, being satis- factory, was adopted. Votes of thanks were passed to the officers far their services during the year.

div.head: i PENKETH.
div.p: i PENKETH.
WINTRY WEATHER AT PENKETH.

Unusually severe weather has been prevalent at this village during the last week. Snow fell heavily on Sunday and Monday, and was followed by a severe frost. The roads are very slippery, and traffic is greatly impeded.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. On Wednesday evening the weekly meeting of the above was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The lecturer was Mr. John Garnett, of Chester. Mr. T. Gandy was in the chair. Mr. Garnett's lectures are always listened to with great attention and pleasure, his bright and lucid description of his subjects being much admired. This week's paper, treating upon heraldry, was no exception. The paper described the origin and subsequent develop- ment of heraldry, and gave much interesting information as to the devices and mottoes seen upon the various coats-of-arms. The lecture was rendered doubly interesting,by the illustrations drawn on the blackboard by Mr. Garnett. At 'the close of the lecture a vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer on the motion of Mr. Parker, seconded by Mr. B. Hobson.

. - Early on Sunday, a sailor named Alexander McLallen met with a shockine death in a small rowing boat on the river Tees at Middlesbrough. The deceased was, one of the crew of the steamer Glasgow, and was assis- log to moor the vessel, when the anchor dropped on Ids head, breaking his neck.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 10, 1892. THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 10, 1892. THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC AT WARRINGTON.
During the week the epidemic has shown no

signs of-renewed outbreali, but it cannot yet be said that it has been completely mastered. The last official report which has been issued shows that from Friday last week to Tuesday this week there were 14 cases. Since Thursday there have been some cases, but how many we are unable to state. IVe are informed that the Health Commit- tee have dec.ded not to issue further reports upon the epidemic because of its rapid abatement. THE LYMM PLACARD.

LETTER FROM THE WARRINGTON TOWN CLERK. At Tuesday night's meeting of the Town Council, Alderman Sutton in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Health Committee, and referring to the-smallpox epidemic,said he scarcely thought that it could be laid to thr charge of the Health Committee that since their appointment they had been so careless and inactive as some very clever people gave them credit for being. Somehow it suited the purpose of some people to-hold Warrington responsible for all the sins and misfortunes ef every town in which the epidemic had broken out, but it must be remembered that Warrington had had thn disease imported, and that other towns where se affected had the opportunity of practically putting in force the lesson they were so apt to teat% Warrington,, when they blamed it for not having put an end to the Infection. They found that even the clever medical men who tried to create a scare by magnifying the danger and warning everybody against dealing with Warrington, did not always successfully practice what they preached, (Hear, hear.) and were no better able to cope with the disease than they in Wirrington. public notice signed by Mr. John M. Fox, medical officer of health at Lymm, purporting to be by order of the Local Board,was calculated,he thought, to do a-great deal of harm to Warrington tradespeople. (Hear, hear.) The Town Clerk had replied according to the wish of the ceremittee, to that public notice of Dr. Fox, and he had a copy of that reply in his hands. Alderman Sutton then read the reply which was as follows : " Town Hall, Warrington, November 30th, 1892.

Dear Sir,—The attention of the Health Committee of beCorporation has been called to an Important Public Notice' which is signed by your Medical Officer of Health and stated to be given By order of the Board,' and referring to the existence of smallpox in this borougn. The notice contains the following statement : Warrington appears now to be entirely in the hands of the enemy ; and smallpox at the present time is running there an almost unopposed career.' This state- ment has been made without full knowledge of the facts, and,, so far as it is intended to reflect upon the action of the Corporation, is most unjustifiable. It seems to have been entirely forgotten by your Board that in 1878 the Corporation of Warrington came to the aid of your town , and stamped out an epidemic of smallpox by the removal of your cases to the Borough Hospital. It is true that this was done under an agreement existing between the twoauthorities at the time, but your Board instead of attempting to assist the Corporation in the discharge of a difficult duty now think it preper to suggest that they enliven-sitting the disease to run an almost unopposed career' in the borough. The notice also states that the town is • soaked with infection.' Comparing the number of eases in Warrington and Lyinm at the date of the notice,, with the population of each district, the propor- tion of cases was about equal, so that if there was any truth in the statement that this town was soaked with infection' it applied with equal force to Lymm. 'rhere are other statements in the notice affecting this town which cannot but have the effect of creating undue alarm and seriously affecting the interests not only of this town but your own, and it does appear strangely inconsistent that notwithstanding the extraordinary precautions recommended by your Medical Officer of Health, the notice which has been so liberally distri- buted, should have been printed in this borough. lam instructed to offer the warmest protest against the un- usual course which your Board has thought fit to take for the protection of your inhabitants in casting asper- sions on the town of Warrington and the conduct of its Authority.—Yours truly, J. LYON WHITTLE, The Clerk, Lymm Local Board." . .

Councillor Skew-GREEN said he should like to say hew much pleased he was to hear that the Health Committee had answered in the bait way they could the placard put out at Lyrnm. Certainly, nothing more damaging in the interests of the town had been published for a long time past, and he thought the same publicity should be, given to the reply which was a masterly answer in his iudgment, as was given to the placard itself. He was also pleased to say that that night there were fewer people in the hospital than there had been for some time—(hear, hear,)—and if the panic which was, caused some time ago could only be continued for a while and the people continued to be vaccinated there would soon be an end of this unfortunate epidemic.

DR. FOX EXPLAINS. At a meeting of Lymm Local Board, on Monday even- ing, the letter was read of the Town Clerk of Warring- ton. This letter will be found in another column. The Town Clerk of Manchester also wrote, complaining of the aetiou of the Local Bond in allowing a nurse from the hospital to go to Manch'Ester.

Dr. Fez rose to make an explanation. He said if the document in question had admitted of being extended, he should have begun it perhaps by saying that " the Local Board of Lymm begs to offer its cordial sympathy with the borough of Warrington in the difficulty in which they are now placed." But that would have been out of place in a document of that kiwi. Hi might have gone on to say that "the Local Board of Lymm admired the extremely urgent efforts that have been made by the Urban Authority of Warrington: to deal with the epidemic of smallpox, with which they are now afflicted." But that would also be out of place. He contended that what he put in the document was simply a statement of facts, as he was told, and which he believed was correct, that the epidemic of smallpox,. in spite of the utmost endeavours of the medical officer, the Sanitary Committee, and other officials, had com- pletely mastered them : that they had no further hospital accommodation, and were obliged to label houses as infected, in order to warn persons from passing through the streets in which they were situated. That was all the information he received, and oaths strength of it he put in a few words what he thought was a literal statement of the facts. However much they might admire the action of the authorities in Warrington—and certainly it was beyond all praise—the smallpox had beaten them, as it would beat the authorities in London and in the most distinguished centres of civilization in Europe He thought the Local Board understood this when they adopted the document. Be did not remem- ber that the Corporation of Warrington. came to their assistance in 1878 in stamping out an epidemic af small- pox. He wag medical officer is 1878. He knew they helped the Board in dealing with an epidemic of scarlet fever., but he did not remember any smallpox. The Clerk said that smallpox was prevalent in Janu- ary and February of 1878. Dr. Fox (continuing), said he commenced his duties as medical officer on the Ist April. The action of the Warrington Corporation in regard to the smallpox epidemic at that time was in accordance with an agree- ment by which the Local Board paid them IFO a year, and they would have gone on paying that up to the present time if the Corporation had granted them one or two beds. The basis of the document referred to was :limply this, that whatever cases of smallpox they had in Lymm at the present moment, whatever difficulties they had been placed in, whatever anxieties they had suffered,and whatever expense the Board had gone to in the matter was all traceable to Warrington ; and he thought it was only right that they should put the peo- ple on their guard against putting their clothes in pawn in Warrington and taking them out again ; or having unnecessary dealings with Warrington—he did not say no dealings at all. As to the letter from Manchester,Dr. Fox said his answer had been already forwarded to Mr. Talbot, the town clerk, and it was to the effect that he was greatly surprised that a gentleman of his ex- perience, and a gentleman with the experience of a Medi- cal Officer of Health should have written such a letter as that on the very, imperfect information they must have received. The nurse mentioned was in Lymm not a few days but a fortnight. She wags most excellent nurse, but le did rather break down in health towards the middle of that period—about the ninth or tenth day. As in so many of these cases of reputed smallpox, she had two pimples. No one would have thought of calling them smallpox if they had arisen under any other conditions, but having these pimples in the smallpox hospital, it was supposed they were connected with the disease. They were dealt with, and never assumed the true "pock" form, nor was her health greatly disturbed. However, an assistant nurse was called in, but she did not seem to make herself happy in the work at all, and nothing would satisfy her but that she and the other nurse should leave at once. It was mentioned to Dr. Williamson and himself, and they said it would not be possible unless they sent for the ambulance from Monsall. However, both nurses were disinfected, and not only a carriage but a train was put at their dispGsal, so that they should not come in contact with anyone. The Chairman expressed himself pleased with Dr. Fox's statement, and expressed his opinion that every precaution had been taken. Dr. Williamson endorsed the remarks of Dr. Fox. The Clerk was instructed to simply acknowledge the letters. Dr. Fox further remarked that by the prompt action centreof tl the Board, in which the e epidemico was not a single case of smallpox in what might be utbreak originallyha d been occurred. confined There was t the e called Lynam village proper. fie wished to mention a circumstance ix bleb was almost incredible. A young man in the hospital, not well enough to gw out, was possessed of a desire to have a new topcoat, and a rela- tive brought him orte into the hospital. He tried it on, and it afterwards went back to the shop, hat the shap, keeper disinfected it, and sent it straight away te4 the

manufacturer. At the suggestion of Dr. Fox, it was decidecl to in- struct the Sanitary Inspector to get the facts of the ca, in order that proceedings might be taken aping the young man and his relatives.

div.head: EXTENSIONS AT WARRINGTON GAS WORKS.
div.p: THE EXTENSIONS AT WARRINGTON GAS WORKS.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD ENQUIRY.

On Wednesday morning an inquiry was held at the Town Hall, by Col. J. 0. 'lasted, one of the Inspectors to the Local Government Board, respect- ing the application of the Town Council to borrow £20,000 for gas works purposes. There were pre- sent the Mayor (Alderman Greenall>, Aldermen Holmes and Wright, Couocillo: s R. T. Fairclough, shaw-Green, Roberts, and Dixon, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. Wilson (assistant clerk), Mr. Haydock (gas enginetr), and Mr. Longdin (surveyor). The Tows CLERK made the following statement : The Corporation acquired the gas works in 1877 and under the Corporation Gas Act cf that year they had power to raise by way of capital a sum of £lOB,OOO. At the time of the acquisitim of the works the capital raised was .£64,000, a capital expeaditure on plant was ..£57,419, £43,000 being left uncalled.- The Corporation paid 25 years' purchase for the under taking, and took over the bonded debt of the company amounting to £5,350. Th. company had power to raise by mortgage a sum of £30,000 aftar the whole of the capital had been issued. The cost of the works to the Corporation was £153,000, being the °vitalised value of the annuities at 25 years purchase, and £5,380 bonded debt,, making a total cost of £1.581350. The Corporation were authorised to borrow £20,0011 for gas purposes, without the sanction of thel.ocal Government Board, such siimito include the capitalised value of the annuities at 25 years purchase, viz., £153,000; leaving a sum of £47,000it0 be borrowed by syto of mortgage, for extensions. Taking the past power to raise additional capital to the extent of £43,000 and power for mort- gage for £30,006 (73,200) less, £47,000 the Corporation had been carrying on the concern with £26,200• LESS CAPITAL THAN THE OLD.COMPANE

had. Of the £4.7,000 the Corporation had borrow ed £43,557, leaving £3,443 unhorrowed. The sum of £43557 had been borrowed during 15 years at therate of £2,903 per annum, and included the sum, of £10,199 paid thor the purchase of 16 acres of land, for new gas works erected at Longford, under power conferred by I the Act obtained in Ina. Under that Act' the Corpora- tion were empowered to borrow with the sanction of the Local Government Board a sum not exceeding £20,000 for gas works purposes. That was a very unfortunate clause, because by the Act of- 1877 they had practically unlimited power to borrow with the sanction of the Local Government Board, and he believed the intentions of the Council in 1879 was to obtain powers to borrow £20,000 without the consent of the Local Government Board, bur in passing the Bill through the House of Commons the words-" with the consent "got inserted. The Corporation had besides purchasing the land established new gas works, with retort house, holder,.and plant. In 1877; according to the estimate filed in, connection with the Bill of that year, the amount required for extensions was £45000,, and at that date the new works since established at Longford were not contemplated. It was proposed to spend that sum in extension.of the old works. In i 875, the Corpor- ation, having in view their-requirements up•to the pr-- sent time, wisely determined to construct new works, as it was then found that the old works would not provide for the reqgirements. The•price of gas when the Cor- poration purchased the works—in 18771 was 4s. per 1000 feet in the borough, and avcording, to distance 6,1. per mile more per I,ooo,fegt, outside the borough ; with allowance for discount—on accounts paid within a month. Since 1877. the Corporation had seduced the price _ _

div.p: num 4s. TO 3s: 613:

making the same allowance for discount as. before. If the reduction had not been made the Corporation would have been L 30,000 better off, and the o.a.s consumers have got the benefit of that sum. The ratepayers had also benefitted by the reduction in the cost of street lighting from £21.45. to £2: per lamp, which meant an annual saving on the rates of over £7OO per annum. The Cor- poration had also established a reserve fund, which now stood at £3,742, and during the 15. years had expended a sum of £2,000 out of surplus profit, on capital expendi- ture. He had a little hesitation in mentioning that sum, lout did so in order to show the Inspector how anxious the Corporation had been to keep down the capital debt, and that for the important reason that their borrowing powers were nearly exhausted. He should mention that in 1890' they obtained a repeal of the section of the Act of 1879, which restricted the price at which the Corpor- ation could redeem annuities at 25 years' purchase, and got power to redeem at market prices • and they had redeemed annuities to the value of £34,000. But un- fertunately for the Corporation the value of the out- standing annuities had been enhanced from 25 to between 28 and 291years' purchase, so that practically the annuities remained as great a liability as before. In 1851 the population of Warrington was 22,894 ; in 1881, 26,894 ;in 1871, 32,144- ;. in 1881, 41,42; and in 1891, 52,742. It was now estimated at 53,000.—Alderman Wright : It will be in excess of that.—The Town Clerk said he put 53,000 to be safe. In 1851 the rateable value was £52,499 ; this year it was £169,441. The Town Clerk, after some conversation with Councillor Green on! the subject, explained that the Corporation's actual INDESTI4IWAESS WAS, £108,195. The Corporation, he said, had gone to the length of t accepting some tendors and entering into a contract for, the work.—The Inspector e: Accepted them provisionally. —The Town Clerk said the work was partly on hand.. Once or twice the town. had been within two or th.
iree-I,

hours of being in total darkness,and the Inspector cOuld thetefore, quite see the reason why the Corporation had entered into the contract for the erection of the newv holder.—ln reply to the Inspector the Town Clerit said it. could be completed before next winter. Re explained, the, items of estimated expenditure constituting the amount sought to be borrowed.

gThONGO TRAINING INSTITUTE, COLWYN BAY, NORTH WALES. Its object is to give Religious and Industrial Education to the most promising of the African Converts in this country, and to es.ablish branch institutions on similar lines I Africa. An earnest appeal is made for £2,000. in order to develop the work. A visit with one of the African Students to any Chur6h or Y.M.C.A. could easily be arranged. RUNCORN WATER BILL. t T A SPECIAL MEEPING of the Improvement Iv Commissioners for the District of Runcorn, held on the 28th day of November, 1892, at the Town Hall, Runcorn, pur- suant to the provisions of the Act 35 and 36 Victoria cap. 91 intituled " An Act to authorise the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in cer- tain cases." The following resolutions were passed by an absolute majority of the said Improvement Commis- sioners. That application be made to Parliament in the Session of 1893 for a Bill to provide for the purchase by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, comp-ulsorily or by agreement of the undertaking of the Runcorn. Weston and Halton Waterworks Company, the winding up and dissolution of the Company, the extension of powers for the Local Govern- ment of the District, the amendment of Acts, and for other purposes. That the costs, chat gel and expenses preliminary and in- cidental to the applying for promoting and passing such Bill Into an Act shall be charged upon the General District Rate. Dated this 30th day of November. 1892. FRED. A. LAKE. Law Clerk.

Richard Burton, of High-at., Flue, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of falsely representing himself to be a bona-fide traveller On Sunday morning, the 26th June last, the defendant obtained si pint of beer from Joseph Tharme, licensee of the Mill House, Dittnn, by representing himself as a tra- veller from beyond the three-mile limit. The defendant, who did not appear, was fined 10s, arid costs 7s. 81.

DRUNKENNRSS. . Knowles, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Croft, on the sth last month.— Fined ss. and costs.—Wm. Moore, Penketh was fined 23. 6d. and costs for drunkenness on the 29th last month.—James Hawkins, drunk at Sankey Bridge on the 7th last month fined 24. 6d. " WHEELMEN "IN TROUBLR. —James Heys, of Great Sankey, was charged with riding a bicycle without a lamp, at 5.20 on the 12ch November. The charge was of a trivial nature and was dismissed.—James Barton of Sankey, was fined is. for riding a bicycle on the foot- path at Buttonwood. As " ENSNA RER " TRAPPED. —George Harrison, a labourer, was fined 53. mid costs for being found upon the land of Mr. John Bridge, Buttonwood, for unlawful purposes, and further with setting a snare on the same ground, for the purpose of ensnaring game. -- RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Sir Richard Brooke Bart., and Mr. James Handley. SHOP DOOM ROBBE RI .—Henry Davies, labourer on the Ship Canal Works, was charged with having on Satur- day night sto!en a jacket and waistcoat, worth 305., from the shop of Timothy Dolan, clothier, Bridge-st. Robert Walker, manager of the shop, saw the prisoner take the articles, pursued and caught him, and gave him into the custody of P.C. Worth.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. DRUNEENNESS.—John Lea, John Clark, and Patrick Corcoran, were each fined ss. and costs for this offence.
